questions.stem: An isosceles triangle \( PQR \) is inscribed in a circle with centre \( O \) of radius 1 unit. Let \( \angle QOR = 2\theta \), where \( \theta \) is acute.

parts.stem: (a) Join \( PO \) and extend it to meet \( QR \) at \( M \). Then prove that \( QM = \sin\theta \) and \( OM = \cos\theta \).
parts.answer: In right triangle \(OMQ\) with hypotenuse 1 and angle \(\theta\): \(QM=\sin\theta\), \(OM=\cos\theta\).
parts.hint: Show all working clearly; match gradients and substitute the given point.
parts.solution:
Draw radii \(OQ = OR = OP = 1\). The line \(PO\) extended meets chord \(QR\) at its midpoint \(M\) and is perpendicular to \(QR\).

In right triangle \(OMQ\), \(\angle QOM = \theta\) and hypotenuse \(OQ = 1\).

Therefore
\[QM = \sin\theta,\qquad OM = \cos\theta,\]
as required.

steps.explain: Draw radii \(OQ = OR = OP = 1\). Because \(PQR\) is isosceles with apex \(P\) and chord \(QR\) subtends \(2\theta\) at the centre, the line \(PO\) extended bisects \(\angle QOR\) and meets \(QR\) at its midpoint \(M\).
In right triangle \(OMQ\): \(\angle QOM = \theta\), hypotenuse \(OQ = 1\). Therefore \(QM = \sin\theta\) and \(OM = \cos\theta\).
Why right-angled at \(M\)? A radius to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord. This connects circle geometry to the trig ratios.
Hence \(QM = \sin\theta\) and \(OM = \cos\theta\) as required.

parts.stem: (b) Show that the area \( A \) of \(\triangle PQR\) is \( A = \sin\theta(\cos\theta + 1) \).
parts.answer: \(A = \dfrac{1}{2}(2\sin\theta)(1+\cos\theta) = \sin\theta(\cos\theta + 1)\).
parts.hint: Show all working clearly; match gradients and substitute the given point.
parts.solution:
Base \(QR = 2\,QM = 2\sin\theta\).
Height from \(P\) to \(QR\) is \(PM = PO + OM = 1 + \cos\theta\).

Area:
\[A = \dfrac{1}{2}\times QR \times PM = \dfrac{1}{2}(2\sin\theta)(1 + \cos\theta) = \sin\theta(1 + \cos\theta) = \sin\theta(\cos\theta + 1).\]

Hence \(A = \sin\theta(\cos\theta + 1)\), as required.

steps.explain: Base \(QR = 2\,QM = 2\sin\theta\). Height from \(P\) to \(QR\) is \(PM = PO + OM = 1 + \cos\theta\) (since \(M\) lies between \(O\) and the chord when \(\theta\) is acute).
Area: \(A = \dfrac{1}{2}\times\text{base}\times\text{height} = \dfrac{1}{2}(2\sin\theta)(1 + \cos\theta) = \sin\theta(1 + \cos\theta)\).
This is the same as \(A = \sin\theta(\cos\theta + 1)\). A common slip places \(O\) on the wrong side of the chord and uses \(1 - \cos\theta\).
Shown as required.

parts.stem: (c) Hence show that, as \(\theta\) varies, \(\triangle PQR\) has its maximum possible area when it is equilateral.
parts.answer: From \(A = \sin\theta(1+\cos\theta)\), set \(A'=0\) to show the maximum when the triangle is equilateral.
parts.hint: Show all working clearly; match gradients and substitute the given point.
parts.solution:
Given \(A = \sin\theta(\cos\theta + 1)\) from part (b).

Differentiate with respect to \(\theta\) and set \(\dfrac{dA}{d\theta} = 0\) to locate the maximum.

Maximise \(A(\theta) = \sin\theta(1 + \cos\theta)\) for acute \(\theta\) in the geometric range. Differentiate using the product rule. \(A' = \cos\theta(1 + \cos\theta) + \sin\theta(-\sin\theta) = \cos\theta + \cos^{2}\theta - \sin^{2}\theta\). Use \(\cos^{2} - \sin^{2} = \cos 2\theta\) and rewrite: \(A' = \cos\theta + \cos 2\theta\). Set \(A' = 0\): \(\cos 2\theta = -\cos\theta = \cos(\pi - \theta)\). Solving in the domain gives \(2\theta = \pi - \theta\) so \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\) (acute solution). Second-derivative or endpoint checks confirm a maximum. When \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\), central angle \(2\theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\) and the three central angles at \(O\) are equal, so the inscribed triangle is equilateral. Hence maximum area occurs for the equilateral case.

Conclusion: as \(\theta\) varies, the maximum area of \(\triangle PQR\) occurs when the triangle is equilateral (matching the required “show that” statement).

steps.explain: Maximise \(A(\theta) = \sin\theta(1 + \cos\theta)\) for acute \(\theta\) in the geometric range. Differentiate using the product rule.

\(A' = \cos\theta(1 + \cos\theta) + \sin\theta(-\sin\theta) = \cos\theta + \cos^{2}\theta - \sin^{2}\theta\). Use \(\cos^{2} - \sin^{2} = \cos 2\theta\) and rewrite: \(A' = \cos\theta + \cos 2\theta\).

Set \(A' = 0\): \(\cos 2\theta = -\cos\theta = \cos(\pi - \theta)\). Solving in the domain gives \(2\theta = \pi - \theta\) so \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\) (acute solution). Second-derivative or endpoint checks confirm a maximum.

When \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\), central angle \(2\theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\) and the three central angles at \(O\) are equal, so the inscribed triangle is equilateral. Hence maximum area occurs for the equilateral case.

questions.stem: Consider the expression \( \dfrac{2 - \sin\theta}{\cos\theta} \) for \( 0 \le \theta \le \dfrac{\pi}{4} \).

parts.stem: (a) Show that \( \dfrac{d}{d\theta}\left(\dfrac{2 - \sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right) = \dfrac{2\sin\theta - 1}{\cos^{2}\theta} \).
parts.answer: Shown as required (see full working).
parts.hint: Show all working clearly; match gradients and substitute the given point.
parts.solution:
Differentiate the quotient \(f(\theta) = \dfrac{2 - \sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\) using the quotient rule \(\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)' = \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^{2}}\).

Working: \(u = 2 - \sin\theta,\ v = \cos\theta\)

Then \(u' = -\cos\theta\) and \(v' = -\sin\theta\). Substitute: numerator of the derivative is \((-\cos\theta)(\cos\theta) - (2 - \sin\theta)(-\sin\theta)\).

Working: \(u'v - uv' = -\cos^{2}\theta + (2 - \sin\theta)\sin\theta\)

Expand: \(-\cos^{2}\theta + 2\sin\theta - \sin^{2}\theta = 2\sin\theta - (\cos^{2}\theta + \sin^{2}\theta) = 2\sin\theta - 1\). Denominator is \(\cos^{2}\theta\).

Working: \(\dfrac{2\sin\theta - 1}{\cos^{2}\theta}\)

Therefore the derivative equals \(\dfrac{2\sin\theta - 1}{\cos^{2}\theta}\), as required. A common slip loses a sign when expanding \(-uv'\).

Working: \text{shown}

Hence the required result is shown.

steps.explain: Differentiate the quotient \(f(\theta) = \dfrac{2 - \sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\) using the quotient rule \(\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)' = \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^{2}}\).
Then \(u' = -\cos\theta\) and \(v' = -\sin\theta\). Substitute: numerator of the derivative is \((-\cos\theta)(\cos\theta) - (2 - \sin\theta)(-\sin\theta)\).
Expand: \(-\cos^{2}\theta + 2\sin\theta - \sin^{2}\theta = 2\sin\theta - (\cos^{2}\theta + \sin^{2}\theta) = 2\sin\theta - 1\). Denominator is \(\cos^{2}\theta\).
Therefore the derivative equals \(\dfrac{2\sin\theta - 1}{\cos^{2}\theta}\), as required. A common slip loses a sign when expanding \(-uv'\).

parts.stem: (b) Hence find the maximum and minimum values of \( \dfrac{2 - \sin\theta}{\cos\theta} \) in the interval \( 0 \le \theta \le \dfrac{\pi}{4} \), and state the values of \(\theta\) for which they occur.
parts.hint: Differentiate first, then evaluate or solve as required.
parts.solution: The correct answer is Maximum \(2\) at \(\theta = 0\); minimum \(\sqrt{3}\) at \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\).

steps.explain: From part (a), critical points solve \(2\sin\theta - 1 = 0\) (since \(\cos^{2}\theta > 0\) on the interval). So \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\) lies in \([0, \dfrac{\pi}{4}]\).

Evaluate endpoints and the critical point. At \(\theta = 0\): \(f = \dfrac{2 - 0}{1} = 2\). At \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\): \(f = \dfrac{2 - \dfrac{1}{2}}{\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} = \sqrt{3}\). At \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\): \(f = 2\sqrt{2} - 1 \approx 1.828\).

Compare values: maximum is 2 at \(\theta = 0\); minimum is \(\sqrt{3}\) at \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\) (smaller than the right endpoint). Why not the endpoint minimum? Because the critical value is lower.
Final answer: maximum 2 at \(\theta = 0\); minimum \(\sqrt{3}\) at \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\).

questions.stem: Find the gradient of the tangent to the curve \( y = \sin x \) at \( x = 0 \).
questions.hint: Use \(y' = \cos x\), then evaluate at \(x = 0\).

steps.explain: What is asked? The gradient of the tangent equals the derivative \(y'\) evaluated at the given \(x\)-value. Why start with differentiation? Because the definition of the tangent gradient is \(m = y'(x_{0})\). A common mistake is to substitute into \(y\) itself instead of into \(y'\).
Differentiate using the standard form \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x\). No chain-rule factor is needed because the angle is simply \(x\). This connects the curve to its slope function.
Substitute \(x = 0\): \(y'(0) = \cos 0 = 1\). Why is this exact? Cosine at 0 is the known unit value on the unit circle. A common slip is writing \(\sin 0 = 1\) by confusing sine and cosine.
Final answer: the gradient is \(1\). This matches the familiar fact that \(y = \sin x\) has slope 1 at the origin (the line \(y = x\) is the tangent there).

questions.stem: Find the gradient of the tangent to the curve \( y = \cos x \) at \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \).
questions.hint: Differentiate first, then evaluate or solve as required.

steps.explain: Goal: evaluate the derivative of \(y = \cos x\) at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\). The tangent gradient is always \(y'\) at the point, not the function value. Connecting: we first need the slope function, then plug in.
Standard derivative: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos x = -\sin x\). The negative sign is essential — forgetting it is a very common mistake and would give \(+1\) instead of \(-1\).
At \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\): \(y'\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = -\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} = -1\). Why? \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 1\) on the unit circle.
Final answer: \(-1\). Check: at the top of the cosine wave the slope should be falling through zero? Actually at \(\pi/2\), cosine is zero and decreasing, so slope \(-1\) is consistent.

questions.stem: Find the gradient of the tangent to the curve \( y = \sin x \) at \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \).
questions.hint: Remember \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), not \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

steps.explain: We need the tangent gradient to \(y = \sin x\) at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\). Strategy: differentiate, then substitute the exact angle. Do not confuse this with evaluating \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\) itself.
Differentiate: \(y' = \cos x\). What this means: the slope function of sine is cosine. A common mistake is writing \(y' = -\cos x\) by mixing sine and cosine rules.

Evaluate: \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{1}{2}\). Why not \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\)? That is \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\) (or \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6}\)). Connecting angle tables carefully avoids this classic swap.
Final answer: \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). The gradient is positive and less than 1, which fits the sine curve between 0 and \(\pi/2\).

questions.stem: Find the gradient of the tangent to the curve \( y = \cos x \) at \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \).
questions.hint: Differentiate first, then evaluate or solve as required.

steps.explain: Goal: gradient of tangent to \(y = \cos x\) at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\). Use \(m = y'\) at that point. Why not use the table value of cosine alone? Cosine is the height, not the slope.
Differentiate: \(y' = -\sin x\). Keep the minus. Connecting: slope of cosine is the negative of sine.
Substitute: \(-\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\). A common mistake is dropping the minus and answering \(+\dfrac{1}{2}\), or using \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\) by accident.
Final answer: \(-\dfrac{1}{2}\). Near \(x = 0\) cosine is decreasing gently, so a negative half-unit slope is reasonable.

questions.stem: Find the gradient of the tangent to the curve \( y = \sin x \) at \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \).
questions.hint: Differentiate first, then evaluate or solve as required.

steps.explain: Find the tangent gradient to \(y = \sin x\) at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\). Strategy: \(y' = \cos x\), then exact evaluation. Note \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\) are equal, but only one option is listed as the principal form here.
Differentiate: \(y' = \cos x\). No chain factor. What this gives: the slope function for later substitution.

Evaluate: \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\). Why positive? In the first quadrant cosine is positive. A common slip is writing \(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) by taking the derivative of cosine instead of sine.
Final answer: \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\). Equivalent rationalised form \(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\) has the same value; match the option text exactly.

questions.stem: Find the gradient of the tangent to the curve \( y = \tan x \) at \( x = 0 \).
questions.hint: Use \(y' = \sec^{2}x\) and \(\sec 0 = 1\).

steps.explain: Goal: tangent gradient to \(y = \tan x\) at \(x = 0\). Strategy: use \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan x = \sec^{2}x\), then evaluate. Why secant squared? It is the standard derivative of tangent (or quotient rule on \(\sin/\cos\)).
Differentiate: \(y' = \sec^{2}x\). Recall \(\sec x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x}\), so \(\sec^{2}x = \dfrac{1}{\cos^{2}x}\). A common mistake is writing \(y' = \sec x\) without the square.
At \(x = 0\): \(\sec 0 = \dfrac{1}{\cos 0} = 1\), so \(\sec^{2}0 = 1\). Connecting: near 0, \(\tan x \approx x\), so slope 1 matches the small-angle behaviour.
Final answer: \(1\). The line \(y = x\) is the tangent to \(y = \tan x\) at the origin.

questions.stem: Find the gradient of the tangent to the curve \( y = \tan x \) at \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \).
questions.hint: Use \(\sec^{2}x = 1 + \tan^{2}x\) with \(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4} = 1\).

steps.explain: Goal: gradient of \(y = \tan x\) at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\). Use \(y' = \sec^{2}x\). Why not evaluate \(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4}\)? That gives the height \(1\), not the slope.
Differentiate: \(y' = \sec^{2}x = \dfrac{1}{\cos^{2}x}\). This is the working slope function for every later substitution.

At \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\): \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), so \(\sec\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \sqrt{2}\) and \(\sec^{2}\dfrac{\pi}{4} = 2\). Alternatively use \(1 + \tan^{2}x = \sec^{2}x\): \(1 + 1^{2} = 2\).
Final answer: \(2\). A common slip is stopping at \(\sec = \sqrt{2}\) and forgetting to square.

questions.stem: Find the gradient of the tangent to the curve \( y = \cos 2x \) at \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \).
questions.hint: Chain rule: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos 2x = -2\sin 2x\).

steps.explain: Goal: tangent gradient to \(y = \cos 2x\) at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\). Strategy: chain rule for cosine of a linear angle, then evaluate. Why chain rule? The inside is \(2x\), not \(x\).
Differentiate: outer cosine gives \(-\sin(\cdot)\), times derivative of inside 2: \(y' = -2\sin 2x\). Missing the factor 2 is a common mistake.
At \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\): \(2x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), so \(y' = -2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} = -2\cdot 1 = -2\). Connecting: at this point the double-angle cosine hits zero and is falling steeply.
Final answer: \(-2\). Check sign: cosine of \(2x\) is decreasing through the point, so the gradient must be negative.

questions.stem: Find the gradient of the tangent to the curve \( y = -\cos\dfrac{x}{2} \) at \( x = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \).
questions.hint: Include both the leading minus and the chain factor \(\dfrac{1}{2}\).

steps.explain: Goal: gradient of \(y = -\cos\dfrac{x}{2}\) at \(x = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\). Strategy: chain rule with the constant factor \(-1\) in front and inside angle \(\dfrac{x}{2}\).

Differentiate: derivative of \(-\cos u\) is \(\sin u\cdot u'\). Here \(u = \dfrac{x}{2}\), so \(u' = \dfrac{1}{2}\). Thus \(y' = \sin\dfrac{x}{2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{x}{2}\). A common slip is forgetting the \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) chain factor.
At \(x = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\): \(\dfrac{x}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\), so \(y' = \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\).
Final answer: \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\). Positive slope makes sense: \(-\cos(x/2)\) is rising through this region.

questions.stem: Find the gradient of the tangent to the curve \( y = \sin\dfrac{x}{2} \) at \( x = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \).
questions.hint: Differentiate first, then evaluate or solve as required.

steps.explain: Goal: tangent gradient to \(y = \sin\dfrac{x}{2}\) at \(x = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\). Use the chain rule for sine of a half-angle.
Differentiate: \(y' = \cos\dfrac{x}{2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\cos\dfrac{x}{2}\). Why the half? Derivative of the inside \(\dfrac{x}{2}\) is \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). Omitting it is a classic error.
Substitute \(x = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\): \(\dfrac{x}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\), so \(y' = \dfrac{1}{2}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{4}\).
Final answer: \(\dfrac{1}{4}\). Do not confuse with \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) — we need cosine of the half-angle, then multiply by \(\dfrac{1}{2}\).

questions.stem: Find the gradient of the tangent to the curve \( y = \tan 2x \) at \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \).
questions.hint: Chain rule factor 2 and \(\sec\dfrac{\pi}{3} = 2\).

steps.explain: Goal: gradient of \(y = \tan 2x\) at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\). Strategy: chain rule — derivative of \(\tan u\) is \(\sec^{2}u\cdot u'\) with \(u = 2x\).
Differentiate: \(y' = \sec^{2}(2x)\cdot 2 = 2\sec^{2} 2x\). Forgetting the outer factor 2 gives half the correct slope — a very common slip.
At \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\): \(2x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\). Then \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), so \(\sec\dfrac{\pi}{3} = 2\) and \(\sec^{2}\dfrac{\pi}{3} = 4\). Therefore \(y' = 2\cdot 4 = 8\).
Final answer: \(8\). Connecting identity check: \(\sec^{2}\theta = 1 + \tan^{2}\theta\) with \(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \sqrt{3}\) gives \(1+3=4\), same intermediate value.

questions.stem: Find the gradient of the tangent to the curve \( y = \sin 2x \) at \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{12} \).
questions.hint: Differentiate first, then evaluate or solve as required.

steps.explain: Goal: gradient of \(y = \sin 2x\) at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{12}\). Use chain rule for sine of double angle.
Differentiate: \(y' = \cos 2x\cdot 2 = 2\cos 2x\). The factor 2 must not be dropped. What this gives is the full slope function.

At \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{12}\): \(2x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\), so \(y' = 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6} = 2\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \sqrt{3}\). A common mistake is stopping at \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) without multiplying by 2.
Final answer: \(\sqrt{3}\). Positive and greater than 1, consistent with a steep rise of \(\sin 2x\) near this small positive \(x\).

questions.stem: Show that the line \( y = x \) is the tangent to the curve \( y = \sin x \) at \( (0, 0) \).
questions.answer: Point \((0,0)\) lies on both; \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x\) so gradient at 0 is 1, matching \(y = x\).
questions.hint: Show all working clearly; match gradients and substitute the given point.
questions.solution:
Let the curve be \(y = \sin x\) and the line be \(\ell: y = x\).

At \(x = 0\), \(\sin 0 = 0\), so the point \((0,0)\) lies on the curve. The line \(y = x\) also passes through \((0,0)\).

Differentiate the curve: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \cos x\). At \(x = 0\),
\[\cos 0 = 1.\]
The gradient of the line \(y = x\) is 1.

Since the curve and the line share the point \((0,0)\) and have the same gradient there, the line \(y = x\) is the tangent to \(y = \sin x\) at \((0,0)\).

steps.explain: What must be shown? The line and curve share the same point and the same gradient there. Why both? A tangent must touch and match slope; matching only one condition is not enough. Strategy: verify the point, then compare derivatives.
Point check: at \(x = 0\), \(\sin 0 = 0\), so \((0,0)\) lies on the curve. The line also passes through \((0,0)\). This connects geometry (shared point) before slopes.
Gradient of the curve: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x\), so at 0 the slope is \(\cos 0 = 1\). Gradient of the line \(y = x\) is 1. They match. A common incomplete answer stops after the point check.
Conclusion: same point and same gradient, so \(y = x\) is the tangent at \((0,0)\).

questions.stem: Show that the line \( y = x \) is the tangent to the curve \( y = \tan x \) at \( (0, 0) \).
questions.answer: Point \((0,0)\) lies on both; \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan x = \sec^{2}x\) so gradient at 0 is 1, matching \(y = x\).
questions.hint: Show all working clearly; match gradients and substitute the given point.
questions.solution:
Let the curve be \(y = \tan x\) and the line be \(\ell: y = x\).

At \(x = 0\), \(\tan 0 = 0\), so \((0,0)\) lies on the curve and on the line.

Differentiate: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \sec^{2}x\). At \(x = 0\),
\[\sec^{2}0 = 1.\]
The gradient of \(y = x\) is 1.

Same point and same gradient, so \(y = x\) is the tangent to \(y = \tan x\) at \((0,0)\).

steps.explain: Show that \(y = x\) is tangent to \(y = \tan x\) at the origin. Need: shared point and equal derivatives at that point. Why both conditions? Either alone is insufficient for a tangent.
Point: \(\tan 0 = 0\), so \((0,0)\) is on the curve and on the line. This is the contact point.
Derivative of the curve: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan x = \sec^{2}x\). At 0, \(\sec^{2}0 = 1\). The line has slope 1. Gradients match. A common slip is computing \(\tan' = \sec\) without squaring.
Therefore \(y = x\) is the tangent to \(y = \tan x\) at \((0,0)\).

questions.stem: Show that the line \( y = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - x \) is the tangent to the curve \( y = \cos x \) at \( \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, 0\right) \).
questions.answer: Point \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},0\right)\) lies on both; curve gradient \(-\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} = -1\) matches the line.
questions.hint: Show all working clearly; match gradients and substitute the given point.
questions.solution:
Let the curve be \(y = \cos x\) and the line be \(y = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - x\).

On the curve at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\): \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 0\).
On the line: \(y = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{2} = 0\). So both pass through \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, 0\right)\).

Differentiate the curve: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\sin x\). At \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\),
\[-\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} = -1.\]
The gradient of the line \(y = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - x\) is \(-1\).

Same point and same gradient, so the given line is the tangent to \(y = \cos x\) at \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, 0\right)\).

steps.explain: Show the given straight line is the tangent to \(y = \cos x\) at \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, 0\right)\). Verify the point lies on both, then compare gradients.
On the curve: \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 0\). On the line: \(y = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{2} = 0\). Shared point confirmed.

Curve gradient: \(y' = -\sin x\), so at \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) we get \(-\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} = -1\). Line gradient: coefficient of \(x\) is \(-1\). They match. Forgetting the minus on cosine's derivative is the usual error.
Same point and same gradient, so the line is the required tangent.

questions.stem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve \( y = \sin x \) at the point \( (\pi, 0) \).
questions.hint: Differentiate first, then evaluate or solve as required.

steps.explain: Goal: equation of the tangent to \(y = \sin x\) at \((\pi, 0)\). Strategy: find slope \(m = y'(\pi)\), then use point–gradient form. Why not just guess from options? Slope errors flip the whole line.
Differentiate: \(y' = \cos x\). At \(x = \pi\), \(\cos\pi = -1\). So \(m = -1\). A common mistake is using \(\sin\pi = 0\) as if it were the slope.
Point–gradient: \(y - 0 = -1(x - \pi)\), so \(y = -x + \pi\). Expand carefully: distributing the minus through \((x - \pi)\) gives \(-x + \pi\).
Final answer: \(y = -x + \pi\). Check: at \(x = \pi\), \(y = 0\); gradient \(-1\). Both conditions hold.

questions.stem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve \( y = \tan x \) at the point \( \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}, 1\right) \).
questions.hint: Differentiate first, then evaluate or solve as required.

steps.explain: Goal: tangent to \(y = \tan x\) at \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}, 1\right)\). Find \(m = \sec^{2}\dfrac{\pi}{4}\), then point–gradient. Why sec squared? Standard derivative of tangent.
Slope: \(\sec^{2}\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \left(\sqrt{2}\right)^{2} = 2\), or use \(1 + \tan^{2} = 1 + 1 = 2\). Missing the square gives wrong slope \(\sqrt{2}\).
Point–gradient: \(y - 1 = 2\left(x - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 2x - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\). Hence \(y = 2x - \dfrac{\pi}{2} + 1\). Watch the arithmetic when expanding \(2\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4}\).
Final answer: \(y = 2x - \dfrac{\pi}{2} + 1\). Verify the point: \(2\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{\pi}{2} + 1 = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{2} + 1 = 1\).

questions.stem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve \( y = \cos x \) at the point \( \left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \).
questions.hint: Differentiate first, then evaluate or solve as required.

steps.explain: Goal: tangent equation at the given point on \(y = \cos x\). Find slope from \(y' = -\sin x\), then rearrange point–gradient form carefully.
At \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\): \(m = -\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\). Dropping the minus gives the wrong half of the option set.
Point–gradient: \(y - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\left(x - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{2}x + \dfrac{\pi}{12}\). Adding \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) yields the intercept terms.
Final answer: \(y = -\dfrac{1}{2}x + \dfrac{\pi}{12} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\). Common error: writing \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\) instead of \(\dfrac{\pi}{12}\) after multiplying by \(\dfrac{1}{2}\).

questions.stem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve \( y = \cos 2x \) at the point \( \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}, 0\right) \).
questions.hint: Differentiate first, then evaluate or solve as required.

steps.explain: Goal: tangent to \(y = \cos 2x\) at \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}, 0\right)\). Chain rule for slope, then point–gradient.
Derivative: \(y' = -2\sin 2x\). At \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\), \(2x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), so \(m = -2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} = -2\). Forgetting the chain factor 2 gives \(m = -1\).
Equation: \(y - 0 = -2\left(x - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\) so \(y = -2x + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\). Expanding \(-2\cdot\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\) carefully produces \(+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).
Final answer: \(y = -2x + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\). Check the point: \(-2\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{\pi}{2} = 0\).

questions.stem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve \( y = \sin 2x \) at the point \( \left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}, \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \).
questions.hint: Differentiate first, then evaluate or solve as required.

steps.explain: Goal: tangent to \(y = \sin 2x\) at the given point. Use chain rule for the slope, then point–gradient form.
Derivative: \(y' = 2\cos 2x\). At \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\), \(2x = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\), and \(\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\). Thus \(m = 2\cdot\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = -1\).
Point–gradient: \(y - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = -1\left(x - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\), so \(y = -x + \dfrac{\pi}{3} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).
Final answer: \(y = -x + \dfrac{\pi}{3} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\). A common error is using \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}\) instead of \(\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\).

questions.stem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve \( y = x \sin x \) at the point \( (\pi, 0) \).
questions.hint: Use the product rule for \(y = x\sin x\).

steps.explain: Goal: tangent to the product \(y = x\sin x\) at \((\pi, 0)\). Strategy: product rule for the derivative, evaluate slope, then point–gradient.
Product rule: \(y' = \sin x + x\cos x\). What each term is: derivative of \(x\) times \(\sin x\), plus \(x\) times derivative of \(\sin x\).
At \(x = \pi\): \(\sin\pi + \pi\cos\pi = 0 + \pi(-1) = -\pi\). So \(m = -\pi\). A common slip is treating the product as if the derivative were only \(x\cos x\).
Equation: \(y - 0 = -\pi(x - \pi)\) gives \(y = -\pi x + \pi^{2}\). Final answer: \(y = -\pi x + \pi^{2}\).

questions.stem: Find, in the domain \( 0 \le x \le 2\pi \), the \(x\)-coordinates of the points on the curve \( y = 2 \sin x \) where the gradient of the tangent is zero.
questions.hint: Differentiate first, then evaluate or solve as required.

steps.explain: Horizontal tangent means gradient zero: solve \(y' = 0\) in the given domain. Why differentiate first? Stationary points are defined by the derivative, not by setting \(y = 0\).
Differentiate: \(y' = 2\cos x\). Set \(2\cos x = 0\) so \(\cos x = 0\). Connecting: zeros of cosine are odd multiples of \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).
In \([0, 2\pi]\): \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and \(x = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\). (Endpoints 0 and \(2\pi\) have \(\cos = 1 \neq 0\).)
Final answer: \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2},\, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\). These are the top and bottom of one full sine wave scaled by 2.

questions.stem: Find, in the domain \( 0 \le x \le 2\pi \), the \(x\)-coordinates of the points on the curve \( y = 2 \sin x - x \) where the gradient of the tangent is zero.
questions.hint: Differentiate first, then evaluate or solve as required.

steps.explain: Solve \(y' = 0\) for \(y = 2\sin x - x\) on \([0, 2\pi]\). The linear term changes the stationary locations relative to plain sine.
Differentiate: \(y' = 2\cos x - 1\). Set equal to zero: \(2\cos x = 1\), so \(\cos x = \dfrac{1}{2}\).
Solutions of \(\cos x = \dfrac{1}{2}\) in the domain: \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\) and \(x = \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\). A common mistake is listing the sine solutions \(\dfrac{\pi}{6},\,\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\) instead.
Final answer: \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{3},\, \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\).

questions.stem: Find, in the domain \( 0 \le x \le 2\pi \), the \(x\)-coordinates of the points on the curve \( y = 2 \cos x + x \) where the gradient of the tangent is zero.
questions.hint: Differentiate first, then evaluate or solve as required.

steps.explain: Horizontal tangents for \(y = 2\cos x + x\) come from \(y' = 0\). Differentiate term by term.
Derivative: \(y' = -2\sin x + 1\). Set \(-2\sin x + 1 = 0\) so \(\sin x = \dfrac{1}{2}\). Watch the sign when solving for sine.
In \([0, 2\pi]\): \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\) and \(x = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\). (Not the third-quadrant/fourth-quadrant pair for negative sine.)
Final answer: \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{6},\, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\).

questions.stem: Find, in the domain \( 0 \le x \le 2\pi \), the \(x\)-coordinates of the points on the curve \( y = 2 \sin x + \sqrt{3}\, x \) where the gradient of the tangent is zero.
questions.hint: Differentiate first, then evaluate or solve as required.

steps.explain: Solve \(y' = 0\) for \(y = 2\sin x + \sqrt{3}\, x\) on the given closed interval.
Differentiate: \(y' = 2\cos x + \sqrt{3}\). Set to zero: \(2\cos x = -\sqrt{3}\), so \(\cos x = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

Cosine is \(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) at \(x = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\) and \(x = \dfrac{7\pi}{6}\) in \([0, 2\pi]\). A common error is taking the acute angles \(\dfrac{\pi}{6},\,\dfrac{11\pi}{6}\) where cosine is positive.
Final answer: \(x = \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\, \dfrac{7\pi}{6}\).

questions.stem: The point \( P\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{1}{2}\right) \) lies on the curve \( y = 2 \sin x - \cos 2x \). Show that the tangent at \( P \) has equation \( 2\sqrt{3}\, x - y = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi\sqrt{3} - \dfrac{1}{2} \).
questions.hint: Show all working clearly; match gradients and substitute the given point.
questions.solution:
Given \(y = 2\sin x - \cos 2x\) and \(P\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\).

Differentiate: \(y' = 2\cos x + 2\sin 2x\).

At \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\):
\[y' = 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6} + 2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3} = 2\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + 2\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 2\sqrt{3}.\]

Tangent at \(P\):
\[y - \dfrac{1}{2} = 2\sqrt{3}\left(x - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right).\]
Rearrange:
\[y - \dfrac{1}{2} = 2\sqrt{3}\,x - 2\sqrt{3}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{6} = 2\sqrt{3}\,x - \dfrac{\pi\sqrt{3}}{3},\]
\[2\sqrt{3}\,x - y = \dfrac{\pi\sqrt{3}}{3} - \dfrac{1}{2},\]
which is the required equation.

steps.explain: Show the stated tangent equation. Strategy: differentiate, evaluate the gradient at \(P\), form the tangent, then rearrange into the given linear form. Why rearrange? Exam “show that” answers must match the printed equation exactly.
Differentiate with the chain rule on the second term: \(y' = 2\cos x + 2\sin 2x\). (Derivative of \(-\cos 2x\) is \(2\sin 2x\).)

At \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\): \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) and \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), so \(y' = 2\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + 2\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \sqrt{3} + \sqrt{3} = 2\sqrt{3}\).

Tangent: \(y - \dfrac{1}{2} = 2\sqrt{3}\left(x - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\). Expand and collect: \(2\sqrt{3}\, x - y = 2\sqrt{3}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{6} - \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{\pi\sqrt{3}}{3} - \dfrac{1}{2}\), as required.

questions.stem: The point \( P\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{1}{2}\right) \) lies on the curve \( y = 2 \sin x - \cos 2x \). Show that the normal at \( P \) has equation \( x + 2\sqrt{3}\, y = \dfrac{\pi}{6} + \sqrt{3} \).
questions.hint: Show all working clearly; match gradients and substitute the given point.
questions.solution:
From the tangent gradient \(m_{t} = 2\sqrt{3}\), the normal gradient is
\[m_{n} = -\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}.\]

Normal at \(P\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\):
\[y - \dfrac{1}{2} = -\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}\left(x - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right).\]
Multiply through by \(2\sqrt{3}\):
\[2\sqrt{3}\left(y - \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = -\left(x - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right),\]
\[2\sqrt{3}\,y - \sqrt{3} = -x + \dfrac{\pi}{6},\]
\[x + 2\sqrt{3}\,y = \dfrac{\pi}{6} + \sqrt{3},\]
as required.

steps.explain: From part (a) the tangent gradient is \(m_{t} = 2\sqrt{3}\). The normal gradient is the negative reciprocal. Why negative reciprocal? Perpendicular lines in the plane satisfy \(m_{1}m_{2} = -1\) (neither vertical).
Normal gradient: \(m_{n} = -\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}} = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{6}\) after rationalising if desired. Use either form consistently.

Point–gradient at \(P\): \(y - \dfrac{1}{2} = -\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}\left(x - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\). Multiply through by \(2\sqrt{3}\) to clear the denominator: \(2\sqrt{3}\, y - \sqrt{3} = -\left(x - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\).
Rearrange: \(x + 2\sqrt{3}\, y = \dfrac{\pi}{6} + \sqrt{3}\), matching the required equation. A common slip is using reciprocal without the minus.

questions.stem: Consider the curve \( y = \sin^{2} x \).

parts.stem: (a) Show that \( y = \sin^{2} x \) has derivative \( y' = 2 \sin x \cos x \).
parts.answer: \(y = \sin^{2}x\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(y' = 2\sin x\cos x\) by the chain rule.
parts.hint: Show all working clearly; match gradients and substitute the given point.
parts.solution:
Write \(y = \sin^{2}x = (\sin x)^{2}\).

Let \(u = \sin x\), so \(y = u^{2}\). Then
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2u\,\dfrac{du}{dx} = 2\sin x\cdot\cos x = 2\sin x\cos x.\]

Alternatively, by the product rule on \(y = (\sin x)(\sin x)\):
\[y' = \cos x\sin x + \sin x\cos x = 2\sin x\cos x.\]

Hence \(y' = 2\sin x\cos x\), as required. (Note also \(y' = \sin 2x\).)

steps.explain: Show the derivative of \(y = \sin^{2}x\) is \(2\sin x\cos x\). Strategy: chain rule treating \(\sin x\) as the inside of a square, or product rule on \(\sin x\cdot\sin x\).
Chain rule: let \(u = \sin x\), so \(y = u^{2}\). Then \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2u\,\dfrac{du}{dx} = 2\sin x\cdot\cos x\).
Alternatively by product rule: \(y = (\sin x)(\sin x)\) gives \(\cos x\sin x + \sin x\cos x = 2\sin x\cos x\). Same result. A common incomplete answer forgets the chain factor 2.
Therefore \(y' = 2\sin x\cos x\), as required. (Optionally note the double-angle form \(y' = \sin 2x\).)

parts.stem: (b) Find the gradients of the tangent and normal to \( y = \sin^{2} x \) at the point where \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \).
parts.hint: Differentiate first, then evaluate or solve as required.
parts.solution: The correct answer is Tangent gradient: \(1\), normal gradient: \(-1\).

steps.explain: From part (a), \(y' = 2\sin x\cos x\) (or \(\sin 2x\)). Evaluate at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\) for the tangent gradient, then take the negative reciprocal for the normal.

At \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\): \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \cos\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), so \(y' = 2\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = 2\cdot\dfrac{1}{2} = 1\). Tangent gradient is 1.
Normal gradient is the negative reciprocal: \(m_{n} = -1\). Why? Perpendicular lines satisfy \(m_{t}m_{n} = -1\).
Final answer: tangent gradient 1, normal gradient \(-1\).

parts.stem: (c) Find the equations of the tangent and normal to \( y = \sin^{2} x \) at the point where \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \).
parts.hint: Differentiate first, then evaluate or solve as required.
parts.solution: The correct answer is Tangent: \(y = x - \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{1}{2}\), normal: \(y = -x + \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{1}{2}\).

steps.explain: At \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\), the point on the curve is \(y = \sin^{2}\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\). From (b), tangent slope is 1 and normal slope is \(-1\).
Tangent: \(y - \dfrac{1}{2} = 1\left(x - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\), so \(y = x - \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{1}{2}\). Expand carefully; do not drop the constant \(\dfrac{1}{2}\).
Normal: \(y - \dfrac{1}{2} = -1\left(x - \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\), so \(y = -x + \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{1}{2}\).
Final answer: tangent \(y = x - \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{1}{2}\), normal \(y = -x + \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{1}{2}\).

parts.stem: (d) Suppose that the tangent meets the \(x\)-axis at \(P\), the normal meets the \(y\)-axis at \(Q\) and \(O\) is the origin. Show that \(\triangle OPQ\) has area \(\dfrac{1}{32}\left(\pi^{2} - 4\right)\) units\(^2\).
parts.answer: Area of \(\triangle OPQ\) is \(\dfrac{1}{32}(\pi^{2}-4)\).
parts.hint: Show all working clearly; match gradients and substitute the given point.
parts.solution:
From part (c), the tangent is \(y = x - \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{1}{2}\) and the normal is \(y = -x + \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{1}{2}\).

Tangent meets the \(x\)-axis (\(y = 0\)): \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2}\), so \(P\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2},\,0\right)\).

Normal meets the \(y\)-axis (\(x = 0\)): \(y = \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{1}{2}\), so \(Q\left(0,\,\dfrac{\pi}{4}+\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\).

Triangle \(OPQ\) is right-angled at \(O\) with legs \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}+\dfrac{1}{2}\).

Area:
\[\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}+\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)^{2}-\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{\pi^{2}}{16}-\dfrac{1}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{32}(\pi^{2}-4).\]

steps.explain: From part (c): the tangent is \(y = x - \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{1}{2}\) and the normal is \(y = -x + \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{1}{2}\). Find the axis intercepts to locate \(P\) and \(Q\).

Tangent meets the \(x\)-axis where \(y = 0\): \(0 = x - \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{1}{2}\), so \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2}\). Thus \(P\) is the point \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2},\, 0\right)\).
Normal meets the \(y\)-axis where \(x = 0\): \(y = \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{1}{2}\). Thus \(Q\) is the point \(\left(0,\,\dfrac{\pi}{4}+\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\).

Triangle \(OPQ\) is right-angled at the origin \(O\), with legs of length \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}+\dfrac{1}{2}\). Why difference of squares? Area is half the product of the legs, and \((a-b)(a+b)=a^{2}-b^{2}\) with \(a=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) and \(b=\dfrac{1}{2}\).

Compute the product of the legs: \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)^{2} - \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{\pi^{2}}{16} - \dfrac{1}{4}\). Then multiply by \(\dfrac{1}{2}\): \(\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{\pi^{2}}{16}-\dfrac{1}{4}\right) = \dfrac{\pi^{2}}{32} - \dfrac{1}{8} = \dfrac{\pi^{2}}{32} - \dfrac{4}{32} = \dfrac{\pi^{2}-4}{32}\).
Final result: area of \(\triangle OPQ\) is \(\dfrac{1}{32}(\pi^{2}-4)\) square units, as required.

questions.hint: Differentiate with the chain rule, then form tangent and normal equations.

questions.stem: Consider the curve \( y = e^{\sin x} \).

parts.stem: (a) Differentiate \( y = e^{\sin x} \).
parts.hint: Differentiate first, then evaluate or solve as required.
parts.solution: The correct answer is \(e^{\sin x}\cos x\).

steps.explain: Differentiate the composite exponential \(y = e^{\sin x}\). Strategy: chain rule — outer exponential, inner sine. Why chain rule? The exponent is not simply \(x\).
If \(y = e^{u}\) with \(u = \sin x\), then \(y' = e^{u}u'\). Here \(u' = \cos x\). Connecting: the derivative keeps the same exponential factor.
So \(y' = e^{\sin x}\cos x\). Common mistakes: multiplying by \(\sin x\) instead of \(\cos x\), or writing \(e^{\sin x + 1}\).
Final answer: \(e^{\sin x}\cos x\). Connecting to later parts: horizontal tangents occur only where the cosine factor vanishes, since the exponential never does.

parts.stem: (b) Hence find, in the domain \([0, 2\pi]\), the \(x\)-coordinates of the points on the curve \( y = e^{\sin x} \) where the tangent is horizontal.
parts.hint: Differentiate first, then evaluate or solve as required.
parts.solution: The correct answer is \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2},\, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\).

steps.explain: Horizontal tangent means \(y' = 0\). From (a), \(y' = e^{\sin x}\cos x\). Why product form helps: a product is zero when either factor is zero.
Now \(e^{\sin x} > 0\) for all real \(x\), so it never vanishes. Therefore \(y' = 0\) iff \(\cos x = 0\).
In \([0, 2\pi]\): \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and \(x = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\). Do not include endpoints unless cosine is zero there (it is not).
Final answer: \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2},\, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\).

questions.hint: Chain rule for \(e^{u}\), then set the derivative to zero.

questions.stem: Consider the curve \( y = e^{\cos x} \).

parts.stem: (a) Differentiate \( y = e^{\cos x} \).
parts.hint: Differentiate first, then evaluate or solve as required.
parts.solution: The correct answer is \(-e^{\cos x}\sin x\).

steps.explain: Differentiate \(y = e^{\cos x}\) with the chain rule. Outer exponential, inner cosine. Track the minus from cosine carefully.
With \(u = \cos x\), \(y' = e^{u}u' = e^{\cos x}\cdot(-\sin x) = -e^{\cos x}\sin x\). Dropping the minus is the standard error.
Final form: \(-e^{\cos x}\sin x\). The exponential factor stays positive; the sign sits on the sine factor.
Final answer: \(-e^{\cos x}\sin x\). Connecting to later parts: horizontal tangents occur only where the sine factor vanishes, since the exponential never does.

parts.stem: (b) Hence find, in the domain \([0, 2\pi]\), the \(x\)-coordinates of the points on the curve \( y = e^{\cos x} \) where the tangent is horizontal.
parts.hint: Differentiate first, then evaluate or solve as required.
parts.solution: The correct answer is \(x = 0,\, \pi,\, 2\pi\).

steps.explain: Set \(y' = 0\). From (a), \(y' = -e^{\cos x}\sin x\). Exponential never zero, so the equation reduces to \(\sin x = 0\).
Solve \(\sin x = 0\) on \([0, 2\pi]\): \(x = 0,\, \pi,\, 2\pi\). Why include both endpoints? The domain is closed and sine vanishes at both 0 and \(2\pi\).
Connecting: these are the max/min of the exponent \(\cos x\), so the composite exponential also has horizontal tangents there.
Final answer: \(x = 0,\, \pi,\, 2\pi\). These match the critical points of the exponent \(\cos x\), so the composite exponential is stationary exactly there.

questions.stem: For the curve \( y = \cos x + \sqrt{3}\,\sin x \):

parts.stem: (a) Find the first and second derivatives of \( y \).
parts.hint: Differentiate first, then evaluate or solve as required.
parts.solution: The correct answer is \(y' = -\sin x + \sqrt{3}\,\cos x,\quad y'' = -\cos x - \sqrt{3}\,\sin x\).

steps.explain: Differentiate term by term. Recall \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos x = -\sin x\) and \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x\). The coefficient \(\sqrt{3}\) multiplies only the sine term's derivative.
First derivative: \(y' = -\sin x + \sqrt{3}\,\cos x\). A common slip is writing \(+\sin x\) for the cosine term's derivative.
Differentiate again: \(y'' = -\cos x + \sqrt{3}(-\sin x) = -\cos x - \sqrt{3}\,\sin x\). Note \(y'' = -y\), which is a useful check later for inflection work.
Final answer: \(y' = -\sin x + \sqrt{3}\,\cos x\), \(y'' = -\cos x - \sqrt{3}\,\sin x\).

parts.stem: (b) Find the stationary points in the domain \( 0 \le x \le 2\pi \), and determine their nature.
parts.hint: Differentiate first, then evaluate or solve as required.
parts.solution: The correct answer is Maximum at \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}, 2\right)\), minimum at \(\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}, -2\right)\).

steps.explain: Stationary points solve \(y' = 0\): \(-\sin x + \sqrt{3}\,\cos x = 0\) so \(\tan x = \sqrt{3}\). Why tan? Divide by \(\cos x\) (where defined).

In \([0, 2\pi]\): \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\) and \(x = \dfrac{4\pi}{3}\). Evaluate \(y\): \(y\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2} + \sqrt{3}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 2\) and \(y\!\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{2} + \sqrt{3}\cdot\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = -2\).

Nature via second derivative (or first-derivative sign): at \(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\), \(y'' < 0\) so maximum; at \(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\), \(y'' > 0\) so minimum. Amplitude 2 matches the R-form \(2\cos(x - \pi/3)\).
Final answer: maximum at \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}, 2\right)\), minimum at \(\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}, -2\right)\).

parts.stem: (c) Find the points of inflection.
parts.hint: Differentiate first, then evaluate or solve as required.
parts.solution: The correct answer is \(\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}, 0\right)\) and \(\left(\dfrac{11\pi}{6}, 0\right)\).

steps.explain: Points of inflection occur where \(y'' = 0\) and the concavity changes. From (a), \(y'' = -y = -(\cos x + \sqrt{3}\,\sin x)\), so \(y'' = 0\) iff \(y = 0\).
Solve \(\cos x + \sqrt{3}\,\sin x = 0\): \(\tan x = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\). In \([0, 2\pi]\): \(x = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\) and \(x = \dfrac{11\pi}{6}\).
At both, \(y = 0\). Concavity changes because \(y'' = -y\) and the wave crosses the axis. A common error is listing the stationary points as inflection points.
Final answer: \(\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}, 0\right)\) and \(\left(\dfrac{11\pi}{6}, 0\right)\).

parts.stem: (d) Hence sketch the curve for \( 0 \le x \le 2\pi \).
parts.answer: Sketch \(y = 2\sin\!\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\) on \([0,2\pi]\): max \((\pi/3,2)\), min \((4\pi/3,-2)\).
parts.hint: Show all working clearly; match gradients and substitute the given point.

steps.explain: Why sketch? Rewrite y = R cos(x − α) or R sin(x + α) with R = 2 shows a pure sine/cosine of amplitude 2. What: draw one smooth wave on [0, 2π] with the stationary points from part (b).
Solution sketch: maximum (π/3, 2) and minimum (4π/3, −2). Crosses the x-axis between these extrema.

parts.stem: (a) What is \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\big(e^{2x}\cos x\big)\)?
parts.hint: Use the product rule \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'\) with \(u=e^{2x}\) and \(v=\cos x\), being careful with the sign on \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(\cos x) = -\sin x\).

steps.explain: Use the product rule \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'\) with \(u=e^{2x}\) (so \(u'=2e^{2x}\)) and \(v=\cos x\) (so \(v'=-\sin x\)).
Factor out the common term \(e^{2x}\).

Option B comes from forgetting the negative sign on \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(\cos x)=-\sin x\). Option C forgets the second product-rule term entirely (only differentiates \(e^{2x}\), treating \(\cos x\) as a constant). Option D swaps which term the factor of 2 belongs to.
steps.work: Compare each distractor to the correct product-rule expansion above

The tangent to the circle at \(T\) is perpendicular to \(OT\), and intersects the \(x\)-axis at \(P\), and the line \(y=1\) at \(Q\). The line \(y=1\) intersects the \(y\)-axis at \(B\).

parts.stem: Show that the equation of the line \(PT\) is \(x\cos\theta+y\sin\theta=1\).
parts.answer: The tangent at \(T\) has equation \(x\cos\theta+y\sin\theta=1\).
parts.hint: The radius \(OT\) is perpendicular to the tangent. Use the point \(T=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\) and the normal vector \((\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\).

steps.explain: \(T\) lies on the unit circle at angle \(\theta\), so its coordinates are \((\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\). The vector \(OT\) (purple) is therefore \((\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\).

parts.stem: Find the angle \(\theta\) that gives the minimum area of the trapezium.
parts.hint: Differentiate \(A(\theta)=\dfrac{2-\sin\theta}{2\cos\theta}\), set the derivative to zero, and check the derivative changes from negative to positive.

steps.explain: Differentiate the area function using the quotient rule. The graph shows \(A\) first decreasing, then increasing.
After simplifying with \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\), the derivative is \(\dfrac{2\sin\theta-1}{2\cos^2\theta}\).
For \(0<\theta<\frac{\pi}{2}\), the denominator is positive. A stationary point occurs when \(2\sin\theta-1=0\).
Below \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) the derivative is negative and above it the derivative is positive, so the area decreases then increases.
Therefore the minimum area occurs at \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{6}\).

questions.stem: Find the indefinite integral: \( \int \sec^{2} x \,dx \).
questions.hint: Derivative of \(\tan x\) is \(\sec^{2}x\).
questions.solution: The correct answer is \(\tan x + C\).

steps.explain: Given: \(\int\sec^{2}x\,dx\). Why start with a standard antiderivative? Integration reverses differentiation of the basic trig forms. What we use is the reverse of \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan x = \sec^{2}x\). A common slip is treating this as differentiation.

Apply the rule carefully. So \(\int\sec^{2}x\,dx = \tan x + C\). Why the coefficient? If the argument is a linear function of \(x\), divide by the inner derivative (chain rule in reverse). A common slip is omitting \(+C\) or writing \(\sin x\).
Check by differentiating the answer: the derivative should recover the integrand. This connects the antiderivative to the original integral.
Final answer: \(\tan x + C\). Include \(+C\) for indefinite integrals.

steps.explain: Find the antiderivative of the function. The integral of \(\sin x\) is \(-\cos x\).
Substitute the upper bound (\(\frac{\pi}{4}\)) and the lower bound (\(0\)) into the antiderivative.
Evaluate the exact trigonometric values: \(\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) and \(\cos(0) = 1\).
Simplify the expression by combining the terms.

questions.stem: Find the value of: \( \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \sec^{2} x \,dx \).
questions.hint: Antiderivative of \(\sec^{2}x\) is \(\tan x\). Evaluate from 0 to \(\pi/3\).

steps.explain: Given: \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/3}\sec^{2}x\,dx\). Why start with an antiderivative? The fundamental theorem says a continuous integrand integrates as \(F(b)-F(a)\). What rule applies? The standard form \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan x = \sec^{2}x\), so \(\int\sec^{2}x\,dx = \tan x + C\).
Write the antiderivative: \(F(x) = \tan x\). A common slip confuses this with \(\int\sec x\,dx\) or with the derivative of sec.
Evaluate at the limits carefully: \(F\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) - F(0) = \tan\dfrac{\pi}{3} - \tan 0\).

Exact values: \(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \sqrt{3}\) and \(\tan 0 = 0\). Therefore the integral equals \(\sqrt{3}\). A common slip uses \(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\) (that is cot, or tan of \(\pi/6\)).
Final answer: \(\sqrt{3}\). Domain check: on \([0,\pi/3]\), cos is nonzero, so \(\sec^{2}x\) is continuous.

questions.stem: Find the value of: \( \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} 2\cos 2x \,dx \).
questions.hint: Integrate \(2\cos 2x\): the 2 cancels the chain factor from the argument \(2x\).

steps.explain: Given: \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4} 2\cos 2x\,dx\). Why treat the constant carefully? The 2 outside multiplies the integral of \(\cos 2x\), and integrating \(\cos 2x\) itself introduces a chain-rule factor of \(\dfrac{1}{2}\).
First find \(\int\cos 2x\,dx\). Let \(u = 2x\), so \(du = 2\,dx\) and \(dx = \dfrac{1}{2}\,du\). Then \(\int\cos 2x\,dx = \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x + C\).

Multiply by the constant 2: \(\int 2\cos 2x\,dx = 2\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x + C = \sin 2x + C\). What this means: the outer 2 and the chain factor \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) cancel. Antiderivative \(F(x) = \sin 2x\).
Evaluate: \(F\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) - F(0) = \sin\!\left(2\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) - \sin 0 = \sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} - 0 = 1 - 0 = 1\).
Final answer: \(1\). A common slip forgets the chain factor and gets \(2\sin 2x\) as the antiderivative, or evaluates \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) instead of \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

questions.stem: Find the value of: \( \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \sin 2x \,dx \).
questions.hint: Antiderivative of \(\sin 2x\) is \(-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x\). Use \(\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\).

steps.explain: Given: \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/3}\sin 2x\,dx\). Strategy: reverse chain rule for sine of a double angle. If \(u = 2x\), then \(\int\sin u\,du = -\cos u\), and we divide by the inner derivative 2.
Antiderivative: \(F(x) = -\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x\). Why the minus? The integral of sine is minus cosine. Why the \(\dfrac{1}{2}\)? From the chain factor of the argument \(2x\).

Evaluate at the upper limit: \(F\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{2}\cos\!\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)\). Recall \(\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\) (second quadrant). So \(F\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{2}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{4}\).

At the lower limit: \(F(0) = -\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 0 = -\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 1 = -\dfrac{1}{2}\). Difference: \(\dfrac{1}{4} - \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{3}{4}\).
Final answer: \(\dfrac{3}{4}\). A common slip uses \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{1}{2}\) instead of \(\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\), or drops a sign when subtracting \(F(0)\).

questions.stem: Find the value of: \( \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \sec^{2}\!\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\,dx \).
questions.hint: Inner derivative of \(x/2\) is \(1/2\); multiply by 2 when integrating \(\sec^{2}(x/2)\).

steps.explain: Given: \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sec^{2}\!\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\,dx\). Why chain rule reverse? The argument of sec is \(\dfrac{x}{2}\), not \(x\). Standard form: \(\int\sec^{2}u\,du = \tan u\).
Let \(u = \dfrac{x}{2}\), so \(du = \dfrac{1}{2}\,dx\) and \(dx = 2\,du\). Then \(\int\sec^{2}\dfrac{x}{2}\,dx = \int\sec^{2}u\cdot 2\,du = 2\tan u + C = 2\tan\dfrac{x}{2} + C\).
Evaluate: \(F\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) - F(0) = 2\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4} - 2\tan 0\).

Compute: \(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4} = 1\) and \(\tan 0 = 0\), so \(2\cdot 1 - 2\cdot 0 = 2\). A common slip forgets the factor 2 and answers 1, or uses \(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) which is undefined (wrong argument: we need \(\tan\) of half the upper limit).
Final answer: \(2\). Continuity: on \([0,\pi/2]\), \(\dfrac{x}{2}\in\left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]\), so sec is continuous.

questions.stem: Find the value of: \( \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \cos\!\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\,dx \).
questions.hint: Antiderivative of \(\cos(x/2)\) is \(2\sin(x/2)\). Use \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{1}{2}\).

steps.explain: Given: \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/3}\cos\!\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\,dx\). Chain reverse for cosine of a half-angle: divide by the inner derivative \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) (i.e. multiply by 2).
Antiderivative: \(F(x) = 2\sin\dfrac{x}{2}\). Check by differentiating: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(2\sin\dfrac{x}{2}\right) = 2\cdot\cos\dfrac{x}{2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2} = \cos\dfrac{x}{2}\).

Upper limit: \(F\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}\). Why \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\)? Half of \(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\). And \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), so this is \(2\cdot\dfrac{1}{2} = 1\).
Lower limit: \(F(0) = 2\sin 0 = 0\). Difference: \(1 - 0 = 1\). A common slip evaluates \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\) instead of \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}\), or forgets the factor 2.
Final answer: \(1\).

questions.stem: Find the value of: \( \int_{0}^{\pi} (2\sin x - \sin 2x)\,dx \).
questions.hint: Integrate term by term: \(\int 2\sin x = -2\cos x\), \(\int\sin 2x = -\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x\).

steps.explain: Given: \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi}(2\sin x - \sin 2x)\,dx\). Why term by term? The integral of a difference is the difference of the integrals. Handle each piece with its own standard form / chain factor.

First term: \(\int 2\sin x\,dx = 2\cdot(-\cos x) = -2\cos x\). Second term: \(\int\sin 2x\,dx = -\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x\). Combining with the minus already in the integrand: antiderivative of \(-\sin 2x\) is \(+\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x\).

Difference: \(F(\pi) - F(0) = \dfrac{5}{2} - \left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\right) = \dfrac{5}{2} + \dfrac{3}{2} = 4\). A common slip drops the double minus when subtracting a negative lower value, or uses \(\cos 2\pi = -1\).
Final answer: \(4\).

questions.stem: These questions recover equations of curves from their gradient functions by integration, using a given point to find the constant of integration.

parts.stem: (a)(i) The gradient function of a certain curve is \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \sin x\). If the curve passes through the origin, find its equation.
parts.hint: Integrate \(\sin x\), then use \((0,0)\) to find \(C\).
parts.solution: The correct answer is \(y = 1 - \cos x\).

steps.explain: Given: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \sin x\), and the curve passes through the origin \((0,0)\). Why integrate? The gradient function is the derivative; recovering \(y\) means finding an antiderivative.
Integrate: \(y = \int\sin x\,dx = -\cos x + C\). Why the minus? The derivative of \(-\cos x\) is \(\sin x\). The constant \(C\) is still unknown.
Use the point \((0,0)\): substitute \(x = 0\), \(y = 0\).\[0 = -\cos 0 + C = -1 + C.\]Hence \(C = 1\).
Equation: \(y = -\cos x + 1\), which is usually written \(y = 1 - \cos x\). Check: at \(x = 0\), \(y = 1 - 1 = 0\); derivative is \(\sin x\).
Final answer: \(y = 1 - \cos x\). A common slip writes \(y = 1 + \cos x\) (wrong sign of cos) or forgets \(C\) entirely (\(y = -\cos x\)).

parts.stem: (a)(ii) The same gradient function \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \sin x\) is used, but now the curve passes through \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},\, 3\right)\). Find its equation.
parts.hint: Integrate, then substitute \(\left(\pi/2,\,3\right)\) for \(C\).
parts.solution: The correct answer is \(y = 3 - \cos x\).

steps.explain: Again integrate the gradient: \(y = \int\sin x\,dx = -\cos x + C\). The family of curves is the same; only the constant changes with the new point.
Substitute the point \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},\, 3\right)\):\[3 = -\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2} + C = -0 + C.\]So \(C = 3\).
Therefore \(y = -\cos x + 3 = 3 - \cos x\). Check: at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), \(y = 3 - 0 = 3\); derivative is still \(\sin x\).
A common slip uses \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 1\) and gets the wrong constant, or confuses with part (i) and keeps \(C = 1\).
Final answer: \(y = 3 - \cos x\).

parts.stem: (a)(iii) What translation moves the curve in part (i), \(y = 1 - \cos x\), to the curve in part (ii), \(y = 3 - \cos x\)?
parts.hint: Compare the constant terms in the two equations.
parts.solution: The correct answer is Translation 2 units upwards.

steps.explain: Compare the two equations: part (i) is \(y = 1 - \cos x\) and part (ii) is \(y = 3 - \cos x\). The trig part \(-\cos x\) is identical; only the constant term differs.
Rewrite: \(y_{\text{ii}} = (1 - \cos x) + 2 = y_{\text{i}} + 2\). Adding 2 to every \(y\)-value is a vertical translation of 2 units upwards.
Why not horizontal? A horizontal shift would replace \(x\) by \(x - a\) inside cos, changing the phase. Here the argument of cos is still just \(x\).
Check at \(x = 0\): part (i) gives \(y = 0\); part (ii) gives \(y = 2\). The graph has moved up by 2. Downwards would decrease the constant; left/right would not match these equations.
Final answer: translation 2 units upwards.

parts.stem: (b) Another curve passing through the origin has gradient function \(y' = \cos x - 2\sin 2x\). Find its equation.
parts.hint: Integrate term by term (watch the chain factor on \(\sin 2x\)), then use \((0,0)\).
parts.solution: The correct answer is \(y = \sin x + \cos 2x - 1\).

steps.explain: Given: \(y' = \cos x - 2\sin 2x\), and the curve passes through the origin. Integrate term by term to find the general solution, then fix \(C\).
First term: \(\int\cos x\,dx = \sin x\). Second term: \(\int -2\sin 2x\,dx\). Since \(\int\sin 2x\,dx = -\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x\), we get \(-2\cdot\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x\right) = \cos 2x\).
General solution: \(y = \sin x + \cos 2x + C\). Why plus cos? The minus in front of \(2\sin 2x\) and the minus from integrating sine cancel.
Through the origin \((0,0)\): \(0 = \sin 0 + \cos 0 + C = 0 + 1 + C\), so \(C = -1\).
Equation: \(y = \sin x + \cos 2x - 1\). Check derivative: \(\cos x - 2\sin 2x\). A common slip keeps \(C = 0\) or writes \(-\cos 2x\) from a sign error.

parts.stem: (c) If \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \sin x + \cos x\) and \(y = -2\) when \(x = \pi\), find \(y\) as a function of \(x\).
parts.hint: Integrate, then use \(y(\pi) = -2\). Remember \(\cos\pi = -1\).
parts.solution: The correct answer is \(y = -\cos x + \sin x - 3\).

steps.explain: Integrate the gradient: \(\int(\sin x + \cos x)\,dx = -\cos x + \sin x + C\).
Solve: \(C = -3\). Therefore \(y = -\cos x + \sin x - 3\).
Check: derivative is \(\sin x + \cos x\); at \(x = \pi\), \(y = -(-1) + 0 - 3 = 1 - 3 = -2\). A common slip uses \(\cos\pi = 1\) and gets \(C = -1\) or \(+3\).
Final answer: \(y = -\cos x + \sin x - 3\).

questions.hint: Integrate, then use \(y(\pi) = -2\). Remember \(\cos\pi = -1\).

Check: derivative is \(\sin x + \cos x\); at \(x = \pi\), \(y = -(-1) + 0 - 3 = 1 - 3 = -2\). A common slip uses \(\cos\pi = 1\) and gets \(C = -1\) or \(+3\).
