questions.stem: Find the indefinite integral: \( \int \cos(x + 2)\,dx \).
questions.hint: Inner derivative of \(x+2\) is 1.

steps.explain: Given: \(\int\cos(x + 2)\,dx\). Why chain reverse? Cosine of a linear expression in \(x\). The standard form is \(\int\cos u\,du = \sin u\).
Let \(u = x + 2\). Then \(du = 1\,dx\), so \(dx = du\). The inner derivative is 1 — no extra constant factor appears.
Therefore \(\int\cos(x + 2)\,dx = \sin(x + 2) + C\). Why not minus sin? Differentiating cos gives \(-\sin\); integrating cos gives \(+\sin\).
Check: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin(x + 2) = \cos(x + 2)\cdot 1 = \cos(x + 2)\). A common slip omits \(+C\) or writes \(-\sin(x + 2)\).
Final answer: \(\sin(x + 2) + C\).

questions.stem: Find the indefinite integral: \( \int \cos(2x + 1)\,dx \).
questions.hint: Divide by the coefficient of \(x\) in the argument.

steps.explain: Given: \(\int\cos(2x + 1)\,dx\). The argument is linear with slope 2, so a chain factor is required.
Let \(u = 2x + 1\). Then \(du = 2\,dx\), so \(dx = \dfrac{1}{2}\,du\).
Substitute: \(\int\cos u\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}\,du = \dfrac{1}{2}\sin u + C = \dfrac{1}{2}\sin(2x + 1) + C\). Why divide by 2? The inner derivative is 2.

Check: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\sin(2x + 1)\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\cos(2x + 1)\cdot 2 = \cos(2x + 1)\). A common slip multiplies by 2 instead of dividing, or forgets the chain factor entirely.
Final answer: \(\dfrac{1}{2}\sin(2x + 1) + C\).

questions.stem: Find the indefinite integral: \( \int \sin(x + 2)\,dx \).
questions.hint: Integral of sin is \(-\cos\); chain factor is 1.

steps.explain: Given: \(\int\sin(x + 2)\,dx\). Standard form: \(\int\sin u\,du = -\cos u\). Inner derivative of \(x + 2\) is 1.
Let \(u = x + 2\), \(du = dx\). Then \(\int\sin u\,du = -\cos u + C\).
Back-substitute: \(-\cos(x + 2) + C\). Why the minus? Differentiating \(-\cos u\) gives \(\sin u\).
Check: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\bigl(-\cos(x + 2)\bigr) = \sin(x + 2)\). A common slip drops the minus and writes \(+\cos(x + 2)\).
Final answer: \(-\cos(x + 2) + C\).

questions.stem: Find the indefinite integral: \( \int \sin(2x + 1)\,dx \).
questions.hint: Minus cos, then divide by 2.

steps.explain: Given: \(\int\sin(2x + 1)\,dx\). Combine the sine integral with a chain factor of 2.
Let \(u = 2x + 1\), \(du = 2\,dx\), so \(dx = \dfrac{1}{2}\,du\). Then \(\int\sin u\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}\,du = -\dfrac{1}{2}\cos u + C\).
Back-substitute: \(-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos(2x + 1) + C\). Both the minus (from integrating sine) and the \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) (from the chain) are required.
Check: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos(2x + 1)\right) = -\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\bigl(-\sin(2x + 1)\cdot 2\bigr) = \sin(2x + 1)\). A common slip flips the overall sign or multiplies by 2.
Final answer: \(-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos(2x + 1) + C\).

questions.stem: Find the indefinite integral: \( \int \cos(3x - 2)\,dx \).
questions.hint: Divide by 3 (coefficient of \(x\)).

steps.explain: Given: \(\int\cos(3x - 2)\,dx\). Inner derivative of \(3x - 2\) is 3, so divide by 3 when integrating cos.
Let \(u = 3x - 2\), \(du = 3\,dx\), \(dx = \dfrac{1}{3}\,du\). Then \(\int\cos u\cdot\dfrac{1}{3}\,du = \dfrac{1}{3}\sin u + C\).
The constant \(-2\) inside the argument does not change the chain factor (its derivative is 0). Only the coefficient of \(x\) matters.
Check: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\sin(3x - 2)\right) = \dfrac{1}{3}\cos(3x - 2)\cdot 3 = \cos(3x - 2)\). A common slip multiplies by 3 or puts a false minus.
Final answer: \(\dfrac{1}{3}\sin(3x - 2) + C\).

questions.stem: Find the indefinite integral: \( \int \sin(7 - 5x)\,dx \).
questions.hint: Inner derivative is \(-5\); two minuses give a positive cos answer.

steps.explain: Given: \(\int\sin(7 - 5x)\,dx\). The inner derivative is \(-5\) (negative slope). Both the sine integral minus and this negative chain factor matter.
Let \(u = 7 - 5x\). Then \(du = -5\,dx\), so \(dx = -\dfrac{1}{5}\,du\).
Substitute: \(\int\sin u\cdot\left(-\dfrac{1}{5}\right)\,du = -\dfrac{1}{5}\int\sin u\,du = -\dfrac{1}{5}(-\cos u) + C = \dfrac{1}{5}\cos u + C\).

Why a plus overall? Integrating sine gives \(-\cos\); the chain contributes another minus (from \(-5\)); two minuses make a plus. A common slip keeps only one minus and answers \(-\dfrac{1}{5}\cos(7 - 5x)\).
Final answer: \(\dfrac{1}{5}\cos(7 - 5x) + C\).

questions.stem: Find the indefinite integral: \( \int \sec^{2}(4-x)\,dx \).
questions.hint: Find an antiderivative, then simplify (add \(+C\) if indefinite).

steps.explain: Given: \( \int \sec^{2}(4-x)\,dx \). Why start with a standard antiderivative? Integration reverses differentiation of the basic trig forms. What we use is chain-rule reverse (inner derivative \(-1\) introduces a minus). A common slip is treating this as differentiation.

Apply the rule carefully. Obtain \(-\tan(4-x)+C\). Why the coefficient? If the argument is a linear function of \(x\), divide by the inner derivative (chain rule in reverse). A common slip is forgetting the constant of integration or the chain-rule factor.
Check by differentiating the answer: the derivative should recover the integrand. This connects the antiderivative to the original integral.
Final answer: \(-\tan(4-x)+C\). Include \(+C\) for indefinite integrals.

questions.stem: Find the indefinite integral: \( \int \sec^{2}\!\left(1-\dfrac{x}{3}\right)\,dx \).
questions.hint: Find an antiderivative, then simplify (add \(+C\) if indefinite).

steps.explain: Given: \( \int \sec^{2}\!\left(1-\dfrac{x}{3}\right)\,dx \). Why start with a standard antiderivative? Integration reverses differentiation of the basic trig forms. What we use is chain-rule reverse (inner derivative \(-1/3\); divide by \(-1/3\) multiplies by \(-3\)). A common slip is treating this as differentiation.

Apply the rule carefully. Obtain \(-3\tan\!\left(1-\dfrac{x}{3}\right)+C\). Why the coefficient? If the argument is a linear function of \(x\), divide by the inner derivative (chain rule in reverse). A common slip is forgetting the constant of integration or the chain-rule factor.
Check by differentiating the answer: the derivative should recover the integrand. This connects the antiderivative to the original integral.
Final answer: \(-3\tan\!\left(1-\dfrac{x}{3}\right)+C\). Include \(+C\) for indefinite integrals.

questions.stem: Find the indefinite integral: \( \int \sin\!\left(1-\dfrac{x}{3}\right)\,dx \).
questions.hint: Find an antiderivative, then simplify (add \(+C\) if indefinite).

steps.explain: Given: \( \int \sin\!\left(1-\dfrac{x}{3}\right)\,dx \). Why start with a standard antiderivative? Integration reverses differentiation of the basic trig forms. What we use is chain-rule reverse (\(\int\sin u\,du=-\cos u\) and divide by \(-1/3\) gives \(+3\cos u\)). A common slip is treating this as differentiation.

Apply the rule carefully. Obtain \(3\cos\!\left(1-\dfrac{x}{3}\right)+C\). Why the coefficient? If the argument is a linear function of \(x\), divide by the inner derivative (chain rule in reverse). A common slip is forgetting the constant of integration or the chain-rule factor.
Check by differentiating the answer: the derivative should recover the integrand. This connects the antiderivative to the original integral.
Final answer: \(3\cos\!\left(1-\dfrac{x}{3}\right)+C\). Include \(+C\) for indefinite integrals.

questions.stem: Find \( \int\!\left(6\cos 3x - 4\sin\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\,dx \).
questions.hint: Find an antiderivative, then simplify (add \(+C\) if indefinite).

steps.explain: Integrate term by term. \(\int 6\cos 3x\,dx = 6\cdot\dfrac{1}{3}\sin 3x = 2\sin 3x\).
\(\int -4\sin\dfrac{x}{2}\,dx = -4\cdot\left(-2\cos\dfrac{x}{2}\right) = 8\cos\dfrac{x}{2}\).
Combine with \(+C\): \(2\sin 3x + 8\cos\dfrac{x}{2} + C\).
Final answer as above.

questions.stem: Find \( \int\!\left(8\sec^{2} 2x - 10\cos\dfrac{x}{4} + 12\sin\dfrac{x}{3}\right)\,dx \).
questions.hint: Find an antiderivative, then simplify (add \(+C\) if indefinite).

steps.explain: \(\int 8\sec^{2}2x\,dx = 8\cdot\dfrac{1}{2}\tan 2x = 4\tan 2x\).
\(\int -10\cos\dfrac{x}{4}\,dx = -10\cdot 4\sin\dfrac{x}{4} = -40\sin\dfrac{x}{4}\).
\(\int 12\sin\dfrac{x}{3}\,dx = 12\cdot\left(-3\cos\dfrac{x}{3}\right) = -36\cos\dfrac{x}{3}\).
Sum: \(4\tan 2x - 40\sin\dfrac{x}{4} - 36\cos\dfrac{x}{3} + C\).

questions.stem: If \(f'(x)=\pi\cos\pi x\) and \(f(0)=0\), find \(f(x)\).
questions.hint: Find an antiderivative, then simplify (add \(+C\) if indefinite).

steps.explain: Integrate: \(\int\pi\cos\pi x\,dx = \pi\cdot\dfrac{1}{\pi}\sin\pi x = \sin\pi x + C\).
\(f(x)=\sin\pi x\).
Final answer: \(\sin\pi x\).

questions.stem: If \(f'(x)=\pi\cos\pi x\) and \(f(0)=0\), find \(f\!\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\).
questions.hint: Find an antiderivative, then simplify (add \(+C\) if indefinite).

steps.explain: From part (i), \(f(x)=\sin\pi x\).
\(f\!\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)=\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).
Final answer: \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).
A common slip uses degrees instead of radians.

questions.stem: If \(f'(x)=\cos\pi x\) and \(f(0)=\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\), find \(f(x)\).
questions.hint: Find an antiderivative, then simplify (add \(+C\) if indefinite).

steps.explain: \(\int\cos\pi x\,dx = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\sin\pi x + C\).
\(f(x)=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\sin\pi x + \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\).
Final answer as above.

questions.stem: If \(f'(x)=\cos\pi x\) and \(f(0)=\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\), find \(f\!\left(\dfrac{1}{6}\right)\).
questions.hint: Find an antiderivative, then simplify (add \(+C\) if indefinite).

steps.explain: Using \(f(x)=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\sin\pi x + \dfrac{1}{2\pi}\):
\(\dfrac{1}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6} + \dfrac{1}{2\pi} = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2\pi} = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\).
Final answer: \(\dfrac{1}{\pi}\).
Check arithmetic with common denominator \(2\pi\).

questions.stem: If \(f''(x)=18\cos 3x\), \(f'(0)=1\) and \(f\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=1\), find \(f(x)\).
questions.hint: Find an antiderivative, then simplify (add \(+C\) if indefinite).

steps.explain: Integrate once: \(f'(x)=18\cdot\dfrac{1}{3}\sin 3x + A = 6\sin 3x + A\).
Integrate again: \(f(x)=6\cdot\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\cos 3x\right) + x + B = -2\cos 3x + x + B\).
\(f\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=1\): \(-2\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{2} + \dfrac{\pi}{2} + B = 1\). Since \(\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{2}=0\), \(B=1-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\). Final: \(-2\cos 3x + x + 1 - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

questions.stem: Find the indefinite integral (\(a,b\) constants): \( \int a\sin(ax+b)\,dx \).
questions.hint: Find an antiderivative, then simplify (add \(+C\) if indefinite).

steps.explain: Given: \(\int a\sin(ax+b)\,dx\). Why start with a standard antiderivative? Integration reverses differentiation of the basic trig forms. What we use is let \(u=ax+b\); \(a\) cancels the chain factor. A common slip is treating this as differentiation.

Apply the rule carefully. \(-\cos(ax+b)+C\). Why the coefficient? If the argument is a linear function of \(x\), divide by the inner derivative (chain rule in reverse). A common slip is forgetting the constant of integration or the chain-rule factor.
Check by differentiating the answer: the derivative should recover the integrand. This connects the antiderivative to the original integral.
Final answer: \(-\cos(ax+b)+C\). Include \(+C\) for indefinite integrals.

questions.stem: Find the indefinite integral: \( \int \pi^{2}\cos\pi x\,dx \).
questions.hint: Find an antiderivative, then simplify (add \(+C\) if indefinite).
questions.solution: The correct answer is \(\pi\sin\pi x + C\).

steps.explain: Given: \(\int\pi^{2}\cos\pi x\,dx\). Why start with a standard antiderivative? Integration reverses differentiation of the basic trig forms. What we use is \(\pi^{2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\pi}\sin\pi x = \pi\sin\pi x\). A common slip is treating this as differentiation.

Apply the rule carefully. \(\pi\sin\pi x + C\). Why the coefficient? If the argument is a linear function of \(x\), divide by the inner derivative (chain rule in reverse). A common slip is forgetting the constant of integration or the chain-rule factor.
Check by differentiating the answer: the derivative should recover the integrand. This connects the antiderivative to the original integral.
Final answer: \(\pi\sin\pi x + C\). Include \(+C\) for indefinite integrals.

questions.stem: Find the indefinite integral (\(u,v\) constants, \(u\neq 0\)): \( \int \dfrac{1}{u}\sec^{2}(v+ux)\,dx \).
questions.hint: Find an antiderivative, then simplify (add \(+C\) if indefinite).

steps.explain: Given: \(\int\dfrac{1}{u}\sec^{2}(v+ux)\,dx\). Why start with a standard antiderivative? Integration reverses differentiation of the basic trig forms. What we use is inner derivative is \(u\); overall factor \(\dfrac{1}{u}\cdot\dfrac{1}{u}=\dfrac{1}{u^{2}}\). A common slip is treating this as differentiation.

Apply the rule carefully. \(\dfrac{1}{u^{2}}\tan(v+ux)+C\). Why the coefficient? If the argument is a linear function of \(x\), divide by the inner derivative (chain rule in reverse). A common slip is forgetting the constant of integration or the chain-rule factor.
Check by differentiating the answer: the derivative should recover the integrand. This connects the antiderivative to the original integral.
Final answer: \(\dfrac{1}{u^{2}}\tan(v+ux)+C\). Include \(+C\) for indefinite integrals.

questions.stem: Find the indefinite integral (\(a\) constant, \(a\neq 0\)): \( \int \dfrac{a}{\cos^{2} ax}\,dx \).
questions.hint: Find an antiderivative, then simplify (add \(+C\) if indefinite).
questions.solution: The correct answer is \(\tan ax + C\).

steps.explain: Rewrite: \(\dfrac{a}{\cos^{2} ax} = a\sec^{2} ax\).
\(\int a\sec^{2} ax\,dx = a\cdot\dfrac{1}{a}\tan ax + C = \tan ax + C\).
Final answer: \(\tan ax + C\).
The constant \(a\) cancels the chain factor from \(ax\).

questions.stem: Find \( \dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x^{2}) \).
questions.hint: Chain rule: outer sin, inner \(x^{2}\).

steps.explain: Given: \(y = \sin(x^{2})\) (written \(\sin x^{2}\)). Why chain rule? Sine of a composite, not \(\sin^{2}x\). What: \(y' = \cos u\cdot u'\) with \(u = x^{2}\).
Product: \(y' = \cos(x^{2})\cdot 2x = 2x\cos x^{2}\).
A common slip confuses \(\sin x^{2}\) with \(\sin^{2}x\), or drops the factor \(2x\).
Final answer: \(2x\cos x^{2}\).

questions.stem: Hence find \( \int 2x\cos x^{2}\,dx \).
questions.hint: The integrand is exactly the derivative from part (i).
questions.solution: The correct answer is \(\sin x^{2} + C\).

steps.explain: From part (i): \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x^{2}) = 2x\cos x^{2}\). The integral asked is \(\int 2x\cos x^{2}\,dx\). Why “hence”? The integrand matches the derivative exactly.
Therefore, by the reverse chain rule (or fundamental theorem for antiderivatives),\[\int 2x\cos x^{2}\,dx = \sin x^{2} + C.\]
Check: differentiating \(\sin x^{2}\) recovers \(2x\cos x^{2}\). No extra constant factor is needed because the match is exact (unlike part (c) where a factor 2 appears).
A common slip writes \(\cos x^{2}+C\) or forgets \(+C\).
Final answer: \(\sin x^{2} + C\).

questions.stem: Find \( \dfrac{d}{dx}(\cos x^{3}) \).
questions.hint: Chain rule: outer cos, inner \(x^{3}\).

steps.explain: Given: \(y = \cos(x^{3})\). Chain rule: \(y' = -\sin u\cdot u'\) with \(u = x^{3}\).
Inside: \(u' = 3x^{2}\). Outer contributes the automatic minus from cosine.
A common slip drops the minus or writes \(3x\) instead of \(3x^{2}\).
Final answer: \(-3x^{2}\sin x^{3}\).

questions.stem: Hence find \( \int x^{2}\sin x^{3}\,dx \).
questions.hint: Relate the integrand to the derivative from part (i); solve for the constant factor.
questions.solution: The correct answer is \(-\dfrac{1}{3}\cos x^{3} + C\).

steps.explain: From part (i): \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(\cos x^{3}) = -3x^{2}\sin x^{3}\). We want \(\int x^{2}\sin x^{3}\,dx\). Compare: the derivative has an extra factor of \(-3\) and the same \(x^{2}\sin x^{3}\) structure.
Divide both sides by \(-3\):\[x^{2}\sin x^{3} = -\dfrac{1}{3}\,\dfrac{d}{dx}(\cos x^{3}).\]What this means: the integrand is \(-\dfrac{1}{3}\) times the derivative of \(\cos x^{3}\).
Integrate both sides:\[\int x^{2}\sin x^{3}\,dx = -\dfrac{1}{3}\cos x^{3} + C.\]
Check: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\cos x^{3}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{3}\cdot(-3x^{2}\sin x^{3}) = x^{2}\sin x^{3}\). A common slip drops the minus or the \(\dfrac{1}{3}\).
Final answer: \(-\dfrac{1}{3}\cos x^{3} + C\).

questions.stem: Find \( \dfrac{d}{dx}(\tan\sqrt{x}) \).
questions.hint: Chain rule: outer tan, inner \(\sqrt{x}\).

steps.explain: Given: differentiate \(y = \tan\sqrt{x}\). Why the chain rule? This is a composition: tan of a square root, not tan of \(x\) alone. What we use is \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan u = \sec^{2}u\cdot u'\) with \(u = \sqrt{x}\).
Differentiate the inside carefully: \(u = x^{1/2}\), so \(u' = \dfrac{1}{2}x^{-1/2} = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\). A common slip forgets this factor and writes only \(\sec^{2}\sqrt{x}\).
Outer derivative: \(\sec^{2}u = \sec^{2}\sqrt{x}\). Multiply by the inside derivative: \(y' = \sec^{2}\sqrt{x}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\sec^{2}\sqrt{x}\).
There is no automatic minus (that would be for cot). The power of sec is 2, not 1. Domain: \(x > 0\) (and where tan is defined).
Final answer: \(\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\sec^{2}\sqrt{x}\).

questions.stem: Hence find \( \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\sec^{2}\sqrt{x}\,dx \).
questions.hint: Compare the integrand with the derivative from part (i); adjust the constant factor.

steps.explain: From part (i) we know\[\dfrac{d}{dx}\bigl(\tan\sqrt{x}\bigr) = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\sec^{2}\sqrt{x}.\]The integral we want is \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\sec^{2}\sqrt{x}\,dx\). Why compare? The integrand looks like the derivative, but the coefficient of \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\) is different.

Rewrite the derivative so the sec–root factor matches the integrand. Multiply both sides by 2:\[2\,\dfrac{d}{dx}\bigl(\tan\sqrt{x}\bigr) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\sec^{2}\sqrt{x}.\]What this shows: the integrand is exactly twice the derivative of \(\tan\sqrt{x}\).

Integrate both sides (or recognise the reverse chain rule):\[\int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\sec^{2}\sqrt{x}\,dx = \int 2\,\dfrac{d}{dx}\bigl(\tan\sqrt{x}\bigr)\,dx = 2\tan\sqrt{x} + C.\]Why the factor 2? Part (i) has a \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) from differentiating \(\sqrt{x}\); the integrand has no that half, so we multiply by 2 to cancel it.

Check by differentiating the answer:\[\dfrac{d}{dx}\bigl(2\tan\sqrt{x}\bigr) = 2\cdot\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\sec^{2}\sqrt{x} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\sec^{2}\sqrt{x},\]which matches the integrand. A common slip is writing just \(\tan\sqrt{x}+C\) (forgetting to undo the \(\dfrac{1}{2}\)) or \(\dfrac{1}{2}\tan\sqrt{x}+C\) (dividing instead of multiplying).
Final answer: \(2\tan\sqrt{x} + C\). Domain: \(x > 0\) where the expression is defined.

questions.stem: Find \( \dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin^{5} x) \).
questions.hint: Write \(\sin^{5}x=(\sin x)^{5}\) and use the chain rule.

steps.explain: Given: differentiate \(y = \sin^{5}x\). Why rewrite? The notation \(\sin^{5}x\) means \((\sin x)^{5}\), a power of sine — not sine of a fifth power. What we use is the power chain rule: if \(y = u^{n}\) then \(y' = n u^{n-1} u'\).
Set the inside carefully: let \(u = \sin x\), so \(y = u^{5}\). Then \(\dfrac{d}{du}u^{5} = 5u^{4}\) and \(u' = \cos x\).
Multiply: \(y' = 5u^{4}\cdot u' = 5(\sin x)^{4}\cos x = 5\sin^{4}x\cos x\). Why keep the cos? Dropping the chain factor is the classic error and would give the distractor \(5\sin^{4}x\).
Structure check: the power drops from 5 to 4 on sin, the coefficient is 5, and cos comes from differentiating the inside. This is not \(5\cos^{5}x\) or \(5\sin^{5}x\).
Final answer: \(5\sin^{4}x\cos x\).

questions.stem: Hence find \( \int \sin^{4}x\cos x\,dx \).
questions.hint: Use part (i): the integrand is one-fifth of the derivative of \(\sin^{5}x\).

steps.explain: From part (i): \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin^{5}x) = 5\sin^{4}x\cos x\). The integral asked is \(\int\sin^{4}x\cos x\,dx\). Why “hence”? Compare the integrand with that derivative.
Divide both sides by 5: \(\sin^{4}x\cos x = \dfrac{1}{5}\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin^{5}x)\). What this means: the integrand is exactly one-fifth of the derivative of \(\sin^{5}x\).

Integrate both sides: \(\int\sin^{4}x\cos x\,dx = \dfrac{1}{5}\sin^{5}x + C\). Alternatively, substitute \(u = \sin x\), \(du = \cos x\,dx\), giving \(\int u^{4}\,du = \dfrac{1}{5}u^{5} + C\) — same result.

Check by differentiating: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{1}{5}\sin^{5}x\right) = \dfrac{1}{5}\cdot 5\sin^{4}x\cos x = \sin^{4}x\cos x\). A common slip writes \(\sin^{5}x + C\) (forgets the \(\dfrac{1}{5}\)) or uses cos in the answer.
Final answer: \(\dfrac{1}{5}\sin^{5}x + C\).

questions.stem: Find \( \dfrac{d}{dx}(\tan^{3} x) \).
questions.hint: Write \(\tan^{3}x=(\tan x)^{3}\); derivative of tan is \(\sec^{2}x\).

steps.explain: Given: differentiate \(y = \tan^{3}x = (\tan x)^{3}\). Why the power chain rule? Tan is raised to a power, so differentiate the outer power and multiply by the derivative of tan.
Let \(u = \tan x\), so \(y = u^{3}\). Then \(\dfrac{d}{du}u^{3} = 3u^{2}\) and the standard derivative \(u' = \sec^{2}x\).
Multiply: \(y' = 3u^{2}\cdot u' = 3\tan^{2}x\cdot\sec^{2}x = 3\tan^{2}x\sec^{2}x\). Why sec squared? Differentiating tan without squaring sec is a common slip (that would give \(3\tan^{2}x\sec x\)).
Structure: factor 3, power of tan drops from 3 to 2, and \(\sec^{2}x\) is required. Not \(3\tan^{2}x\) alone, and not \(3\tan x\sec^{2}x\).
Final answer: \(3\tan^{2}x\sec^{2}x\).

questions.stem: Hence find \( \int \tan^{2}x\sec^{2}x\,dx \).
questions.hint: Part (i) shows the integrand is one-third of the derivative of \(\tan^{3}x\).

steps.explain: From part (i): \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(\tan^{3}x) = 3\tan^{2}x\sec^{2}x\). The integral is \(\int\tan^{2}x\sec^{2}x\,dx\). Compare coefficients: the derivative has an extra factor of 3.
Divide both sides by 3: \(\tan^{2}x\sec^{2}x = \dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{d}{dx}(\tan^{3}x)\). What this means: the integrand is one-third the derivative of \(\tan^{3}x\).

Integrate: \(\int\tan^{2}x\sec^{2}x\,dx = \dfrac{1}{3}\tan^{3}x + C\). Substitution check: let \(u = \tan x\), then \(du = \sec^{2}x\,dx\), so \(\int u^{2}\,du = \dfrac{1}{3}u^{3} + C\) — same answer.

Differentiate to verify: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\tan^{3}x\right) = \dfrac{1}{3}\cdot 3\tan^{2}x\sec^{2}x = \tan^{2}x\sec^{2}x\). A common slip writes \(\tan^{3}x + C\) or confuses with \(\sec^{3}x\).
Final answer: \(\dfrac{1}{3}\tan^{3}x + C\).

questions.stem: Differentiate \( e^{\sin x} \).
questions.hint: Chain rule: derivative of \(e^{u}\) is \(e^{u}\cdot u'\).
questions.solution: The correct answer is \(e^{\sin x}\cos x\).

steps.explain: Given: differentiate \(y = e^{\sin x}\). Why chain rule? The exponential is of a non-linear function of \(x\). What: if \(y = e^{u}\) then \(y' = e^{u}\cdot u'\).
Let \(u = \sin x\). Then \(u' = \cos x\), and the exponential factor stays \(e^{u} = e^{\sin x}\).

Multiply: \(y' = e^{\sin x}\cdot\cos x = e^{\sin x}\cos x\). Why not multiply by sin? The inside derivative of sin is cos, not sin. A common slip writes \(e^{\sin x}\sin x\) or forgets the chain factor entirely and writes only \(e^{\sin x}\).
Sign note: there is no automatic minus (that would appear for \(e^{\cos x}\) or for differentiating cos). The form is positive cos times the exponential.
Final answer: \(e^{\sin x}\cos x\).

questions.stem: Hence find \( \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \cos x\, e^{\sin x}\,dx \).
questions.hint: The integrand is the derivative of \(e^{\sin x}\) from part (i).

steps.explain: From part (i): \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\bigl(e^{\sin x}\bigr) = e^{\sin x}\cos x\). The definite integral is \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \cos x\, e^{\sin x}\,dx\). Why “hence”? The integrand is exactly that derivative.
By the fundamental theorem, the antiderivative is \(e^{\sin x}\). No extra constant factor is needed because the match with part (i) is exact.
Evaluate: \(F\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) - F(0) = e^{\sin(\pi/2)} - e^{\sin 0} = e^{1} - e^{0} = e - 1\).
A common slip writes \(e\) only (forgets to subtract the lower limit \(e^{0} = 1\)), or adds \(+C\) to a definite integral, or confuses \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) with 0.
Final answer: \(e - 1\).

questions.stem: Differentiate \( e^{\tan x} \).
questions.hint: Chain rule with inside tan; derivative of tan is \(\sec^{2}x\).

steps.explain: To differentiate \( y = e^{\tan x} \), we need to use the chain rule. Let \( u = \tan x \), so \( y = e^u \).
First, differentiate the outer function \( y = e^u \) with respect to \( u \).
Next, differentiate the inner function \( u = \tan x \) with respect to \( x \).
Multiply them together to find the final derivative.

questions.stem: Hence find \( \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \sec^{2}x\, e^{\tan x}\,dx \).
questions.hint: The integrand matches the derivative of \(e^{\tan x}\) from part (i).

steps.explain: From part (i): \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\bigl(e^{\tan x}\bigr) = e^{\tan x}\sec^{2}x\). The integral is \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/4} \sec^{2}x\, e^{\tan x}\,dx\) — exact match.
Antiderivative: \(F(x) = e^{\tan x}\).
Evaluate: \(F\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) - F(0) = e^{\tan(\pi/4)} - e^{\tan 0} = e^{1} - e^{0} = e - 1\). Why \(\pi/4\)? Because \(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4} = 1\), so the upper value is exactly \(e\).
A common slip uses \(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\) or forgets the lower limit \(e^{0} = 1\).
Final answer: \(e - 1\).

questions.stem: Given that \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x - x\cos x)=x\sin x\), find \( \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} x\sin x \,dx \).
questions.hint: Use the given antiderivative and evaluate \(F(\pi/2) - F(0)\).

steps.explain: Given that \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x - x\cos x) = x\sin x\). What this means: an antiderivative of the integrand \(x\sin x\) is \(F(x) = \sin x - x\cos x\). Why trust it? You may verify by product rule if required: derivative of \(-x\cos x\) plus cos recovers \(x\sin x\).
By the fundamental theorem: \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2} x\sin x\,dx = F\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) - F(0)\).
At the upper limit: \(F\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 1 - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\cdot 0 = 1\).
At the lower limit: \(F(0) = \sin 0 - 0\cdot\cos 0 = 0\). Difference: \(1 - 0 = 1\). A common slip forgets the \(-x\cos x\) term at 0 (still 0) or incorrectly uses \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 1\).
Final answer: \(1\).

questions.stem: Given that \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\!\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\cos^{3}x - \cos x\right)=\sin^{3}x\), find \( \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \sin^{3}x \,dx \).
questions.hint: Evaluate the given antiderivative at \(\pi/3\) and at 0; subtract carefully.

steps.explain: Given that \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\!\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\cos^{3}x - \cos x\right) = \sin^{3}x\). So an antiderivative is \(F(x) = \dfrac{1}{3}\cos^{3}x - \cos x\).

We need \(F\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) - F(0)\). First the upper value: \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), so \(\cos^{3}\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{1}{8}\). Thus \(F\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{3}\cdot\dfrac{1}{8} - \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{24} - \dfrac{1}{2}\).
Lower value: \(\cos 0 = 1\), so \(F(0) = \dfrac{1}{3}\cdot 1 - 1 = \dfrac{1}{3} - 1 = -\dfrac{2}{3}\).
Difference with a common denominator 24: \(\dfrac{1}{24} - \dfrac{1}{2} - \left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{24} - \dfrac{12}{24} + \dfrac{16}{24} = \dfrac{1 - 12 + 16}{24} = \dfrac{5}{24}\).
Final answer: \(\dfrac{5}{24}\). A common slip drops the double minus when subtracting \(F(0)\), or uses \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

questions.stem: A given differentiation identity can be used to evaluate a related definite integral of a product involving a trig function.

parts.stem: Given \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\!\left(\dfrac{1}{2}x\sin 2x + \dfrac{1}{4}\cos 2x\right)=x\cos 2x\), find \( \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} x\cos 2x \,dx \).
parts.hint: Use the given antiderivative; evaluate carefully at \(\pi/4\) and 0 (watch the double-angle).
parts.solution: The correct answer is \(\dfrac{\pi}{8} - \dfrac{1}{4}\).

steps.explain: Given that \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\!\left(\dfrac{1}{2}x\sin 2x + \dfrac{1}{4}\cos 2x\right) = x\cos 2x\). What this means: an antiderivative of the integrand \(x\cos 2x\) is\[F(x) = \dfrac{1}{2}x\sin 2x + \dfrac{1}{4}\cos 2x.\]Why “given”? You do not need to re-derive integration by parts; use \(F\) directly.
The definite integral is \(F\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) - F(0)\). Start with the upper limit. First compute the double angle: \(2\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

At \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\): \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 1\) and \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 0\). So\[F\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4}\cdot 1 + \dfrac{1}{4}\cdot 0 = \dfrac{\pi}{8}.\]
At \(x = 0\): \(\sin 0 = 0\) and \(\cos 0 = 1\). So\[F(0) = \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 0\cdot 0 + \dfrac{1}{4}\cdot 1 = \dfrac{1}{4}.\]
Subtract: \(\dfrac{\pi}{8} - \dfrac{1}{4}\). A common slip adds the terms (getting \(\dfrac{\pi}{8}+\dfrac{1}{4}\)), or evaluates \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) instead of \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).
Final answer: \(\dfrac{\pi}{8} - \dfrac{1}{4}\).

questions.stem: Given \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\!\left(\dfrac{1}{2}x\sin 2x + \dfrac{1}{4}\cos 2x\right)=x\cos 2x\), find \( \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} x\cos 2x \,dx \).
questions.hint: Use the given antiderivative; evaluate carefully at \(\pi/4\) and 0 (watch the double-angle).

steps.explain: Given that \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\!\left(\dfrac{1}{2}x\sin 2x + \dfrac{1}{4}\cos 2x\right) = x\cos 2x\). What this means: an antiderivative of the integrand \(x\cos 2x\) is\[F(x) = \dfrac{1}{2}x\sin 2x + \dfrac{1}{4}\cos 2x.\]Why “given”? You do not need to re-derive integration by parts; use \(F\) directly.
The definite integral is \(F\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) - F(0)\). Start with the upper limit. First compute the double angle: \(2\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

At \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\): \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 1\) and \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 0\). So\[F\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4}\cdot 1 + \dfrac{1}{4}\cdot 0 = \dfrac{\pi}{8}.\]
At \(x = 0\): \(\sin 0 = 0\) and \(\cos 0 = 1\). So\[F(0) = \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 0\cdot 0 + \dfrac{1}{4}\cdot 1 = \dfrac{1}{4}.\]
Subtract: \(\dfrac{\pi}{8} - \dfrac{1}{4}\). A common slip adds the terms (getting \(\dfrac{\pi}{8}+\dfrac{1}{4}\)), or evaluates \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) instead of \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).
Final answer: \(\dfrac{\pi}{8} - \dfrac{1}{4}\).

questions.stem: Does the definite integral \( \int_{0}^{\pi} \sec^{2} x \,dx \) exist? If so, find its value; if not, choose the correct reason.
options: Does not exist: \(\sec^{2}x\) has a vertical asymptote at \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) in the interval
Does not exist: the antiderivative is undefined at 0
questions.hint: Check continuity of the integrand on the whole closed interval.
questions.solution: The integral does not exist: \(\sec^{2}x\) has a vertical asymptote at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) in the interval.

steps.explain: The formal antiderivative of \(\sec^{2}x\) is \(\tan x\). Why is that not enough? The fundamental theorem requires the integrand to be continuous on the closed interval of integration (or at least improperly integrable).

On \([0,\pi]\), look for discontinuities: \(\sec x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x}\) blows up where \(\cos x = 0\). In this interval, \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 0\), so \(\sec^{2}x\) has a vertical asymptote at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).
Because the singularity lies strictly inside \([0,\pi]\), the ordinary definite integral \(\int_{0}^{\pi}\sec^{2}x\,dx\) does not exist.
steps.work: \text{does not exist as a proper definite integral}

steps.explain: A common trap is to write \(\tan\pi - \tan 0 = 0 - 0 = 0\). This is invalid: the FTC does not apply across an asymptote, even if the formal endpoint values of the antiderivative look fine.
Final answer: does not exist — vertical asymptote of \(\sec^{2}x\) at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

questions.stem: Does the definite integral \( \int_{0}^{\pi} \tan x \,dx \) exist?
options: Does not exist: \(\tan x\) is discontinuous at \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) in the interval
Does not exist: tan is odd
questions.hint: Tan has a vertical asymptote where cos is zero.
questions.solution: The integral does not exist: \(\tan x\) is discontinuous at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) in the interval.

steps.explain: Consider \(\int_{0}^{\pi}\tan x\,dx\). A formal antiderivative is \(-\ln|\cos x|\) (or \(\ln|\sec x|\)). Again, first check continuity of the integrand.
On \([0,\pi]\), \(\tan x\) is discontinuous at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) (vertical asymptote where \(\cos x = 0\)). The integrand is not continuous on the whole interval.
Therefore the ordinary definite integral does not exist. (Improper “principal value” tricks are not required for this question.)
A common slip claims the integral is 0 because tan is “odd about \(\pi/2\)” without justifying improper convergence — that is not accepted as existence of the standard definite integral here.
Final answer: does not exist — discontinuity of \(\tan x\) at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

questions.stem: Does the definite integral \( \int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \cot x \,dx \) exist?
options: Exists and equals \(\ln|\sin x|\) evaluated at the ends
Does not exist: \(\cot x\) is discontinuous at \(x=0\) in the interval
Does not exist: cot is undefined at both endpoints only
questions.hint: Cot has a vertical asymptote where sin is zero.
questions.solution: The integral does not exist: \(\cot x\) is discontinuous at \(x = 0\) in the interval.

steps.explain: Consider \(\displaystyle\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cot x\,dx\). Formally, \(\int\cot x\,dx = \ln|\sin x| + C\). First check continuity on the interval.

Cotangent has a vertical asymptote at \(x = 0\) (where \(\sin x = 0\)), and 0 lies strictly inside \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\). So the integrand is not continuous on the whole interval.

Although cot is an odd function, an odd singularity in the middle does not automatically make the improper integral exist in the ordinary sense required here. The definite integral is not defined as a standard Riemann integral on this interval.
Additionally, cot is undefined at the endpoints \(x = \pm\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) (where cos is zero). That reinforces that the closed-interval setup is invalid.
Final answer: does not exist — discontinuity of \(\cot x\) at \(x = 0\) (inside the interval).

questions.stem: Use trigonometric identities to evaluate the following integrals.

parts.stem: (a) Copy and complete \(1 + \tan^{2}x = \dots\), and hence find \(\int \tan^{2}x\,dx\).
parts.hint: Use \(1+\tan^{2}x=\sec^{2}x\), then integrate \(\sec^{2}x-1\).
parts.solution: The correct answer is \(\tan x - x + C\).

steps.explain: Start from the Pythagorean identity: \(1 + \tan^{2}x = \sec^{2}x\). Why this identity? There is no elementary standard form for \(\int\tan^{2}x\,dx\) by itself, but \(\sec^{2}x\) is the derivative of \(\tan x\).
Rearrange for the integrand: \(\tan^{2}x = \sec^{2}x - 1\). What this does: rewrites the integral as a sum of two standard pieces.
Integrate term by term: \(\int\tan^{2}x\,dx = \int(\sec^{2}x - 1)\,dx = \tan x - x + C\). Why \(+C\)? Indefinite integrals always include an arbitrary constant.
Check by differentiating: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(\tan x - x) = \sec^{2}x - 1 = \tan^{2}x\). A common slip is writing \(\tan x + x + C\) (wrong sign on \(x\)) or integrating tan as if it were sec.
Final answer: \(\tan x - x + C\). The completed identity is \(1+\tan^{2}x=\sec^{2}x\).

parts.stem: (b) Simplify \(1 - \sin^{2}x\), and hence find the value of \(\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \dfrac{2}{1-\sin^{2}x}\,dx\).
parts.hint: Rewrite as \(2\sec^{2}x\), then evaluate \(2\tan x\) at the limits.
parts.solution: The correct answer is \(2\sqrt{3}\).

steps.explain: Simplify the denominator using a Pythagorean identity: \(1 - \sin^{2}x = \cos^{2}x\). Why? Then the fraction becomes a multiple of a standard derivative.
Rewrite the integrand: \(\dfrac{2}{1-\sin^{2}x} = \dfrac{2}{\cos^{2}x} = 2\sec^{2}x\). What this means: the integral is twice the integral of \(\sec^{2}x\).
Antiderivative: \(\int 2\sec^{2}x\,dx = 2\tan x\). A common slip forgets the factor 2 or uses \(\sin\) instead of \(\tan\).
Evaluate from 0 to \(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\): \(2\tan\dfrac{\pi}{3} - 2\tan 0 = 2\sqrt{3} - 0 = 2\sqrt{3}\).
Final answer: \(2\sqrt{3}\). Domain note: on \([0,\pi/3]\), \(\cos x \neq 0\), so the integrand is continuous.

questions.stem: The standard form \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx = \ln|f(x)| + C\) is useful for many trig integrals.

parts.stem: (a) Copy and complete: \(\displaystyle\int \dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx = \dots\)
parts.hint: Substitute \(u=f(x)\) so the integral becomes \(\int\dfrac{1}{u}\,du\).
parts.solution: The correct answer is \(\ln|f(x)| + C\).

steps.explain: This is the standard log form of the chain rule in reverse. Why? If \(u = f(x)\), then \(du = f'(x)\,dx\), so the integrand becomes \(\dfrac{1}{u}\,du\).
Integrate: \(\int\dfrac{1}{u}\,du = \ln|u| + C\). Substituting back gives \(\ln|f(x)| + C\).
Why absolute value? The logarithm of a real number requires a positive argument; \(|f(x)|\) covers intervals where \(f\) is negative (and nonzero).
A common slip writes \(\dfrac{1}{f(x)}\) (confusing with the power rule) or drops the absolute value and the constant \(C\).
Final answer: \(\ln|f(x)| + C\).

parts.stem: (b) Hence find the exact value of \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \dfrac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}\,dx\).
parts.hint: Use part (a) with \(f(x)=1+\sin x\).
parts.solution: The correct answer is \(\ln\dfrac{3}{2}\).

steps.explain: From part (a), look for the form \(\dfrac{f'}{f}\). Here the denominator is \(1+\sin x\) and its derivative is \(\cos x\), which is exactly the numerator. So \(f(x)=1+\sin x\).
Therefore the indefinite integral is \(\ln|1+\sin x| + C\). On \([0,\pi/6]\), \(1+\sin x > 0\), so absolute values may be dropped for evaluation.
Evaluate: \(\ln\!\left(1+\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) - \ln(1+\sin 0) = \ln\!\left(1+\dfrac{1}{2}\right) - \ln(1+0) = \ln\dfrac{3}{2} - \ln 1 = \ln\dfrac{3}{2}\).
Numerical check: \(\ln\dfrac{3}{2} \approx 0.405 \approx 0.4\), matching the “approximately 0.4” form of the original show-that statement. The exact value is preferred.
Final answer: \(\ln\dfrac{3}{2}\). A common slip uses \(f=\sin x\) only and gets the wrong limits.

parts.stem: (a) Using \(\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\), the value of \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \tan x\,dx\) is:
parts.hint: Substitute \(u=\cos x\); remember the minus from \(du\).
parts.solution: The correct answer is \(\dfrac{1}{2}\ln 2\).

steps.explain: Rewrite the integrand: \(\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\). Strategy: substitute so that the numerator is (up to a sign) the derivative of the denominator.
Let \(u = \cos x\). Then \(du = -\sin x\,dx\), so \(\sin x\,dx = -\,du\). The integral becomes \(\int\dfrac{-du}{u} = -\ln|u| + C = -\ln|\cos x| + C\) (equivalently \(\ln|\sec x| + C\)).
Definite integral from 0 to \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\): \([-\ln|\cos x|]_{0}^{\pi/4} = \left(-\ln\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) - \left(-\ln\cos 0\right)\).
Simplify: \(-\ln 2^{-1/2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\ln 2\) (since \(\ln 1 = 0\)). Why positive? On \((0,\pi/4)\), tan is positive, so the integral must be positive — reject \(-\dfrac{1}{2}\ln 2\).
Final answer: \(\dfrac{1}{2}\ln 2\). A common slip drops the factor \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) from \(\ln\sqrt{2}\).

parts.stem: (b) Using \(\cot x = \dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\), find \(\displaystyle\int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \cot x\,dx\).
parts.hint: Substitute \(u=\sin x\).
parts.solution: The correct answer is \(\ln 2\).

steps.explain: Rewrite: \(\cot x = \dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\). Let \(u = \sin x\), then \(du = \cos x\,dx\). So \(\int\cot x\,dx = \int\dfrac{1}{u}\,du = \ln|u| + C = \ln|\sin x| + C\).
Why no extra minus here? Unlike tan, the numerator is already the derivative of the denominator (with a plus). A common slip copies the tan substitution and inserts a false minus.
Evaluate from \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\) to \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\): \(\ln\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \ln\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6} = \ln 1 - \ln\dfrac{1}{2} = 0 - (-\ln 2) = \ln 2\).
Sign check: on \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\), cot is positive, so the integral is positive. Reject \(-\ln 2\).
Final answer: \(\ln 2\).

questions.stem: A trigonometric function \(f(x)\) satisfies \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} f(x)\,dx \ne \int_{\pi/2}^{\pi} f(x)\,dx\). Which function could be \(f(x)\)?
questions.hint: Sketch each function over \([0,\pi]\) and check whether the area from \(0\) to \(\pi/2\) visually matches the area from \(\pi/2\) to \(\pi\) (accounting for sign).

steps.explain: For \(\sin x\): it is symmetric about \(x=\pi/2\) over \([0,\pi]\), so the two areas are equal (both positive and mirror images) — this does NOT satisfy the condition.

For \(\cos(2x)\) and \(\cos(4x)\): both complete an integer or half-integer number of symmetric cycles over \([0,\pi]\) such that the two half-interval integrals work out equal in magnitude — checking each confirms they do NOT satisfy the condition either.

For \(\sin(2x)\): over \([0,\pi/2]\), it completes one full positive hump (period \(\pi\), so \([0,\pi/2]\) is exactly half a period — a positive hump); over \([\pi/2,\pi]\), it is a negative hump of the same shape. The two integrals have opposite sign and are therefore unequal (one positive, one negative) unless both are zero — direct calculation confirms they are unequal in general.

questions.hint: Use \(\int\cos x = \sin x\); \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

steps.explain: The function \( y = \cos x \) is non-negative on \( [\pi/3, \pi/2] \). Set up the integral.
Find the antiderivative.
Apply the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

questions.hint: Integrate: \(\int\cos 3x\,dx = \dfrac{1}{3}\sin 3x\). Then use \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}=1\) and \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\).

Find the antiderivative.

questions.stem: Find the exact area enclosed between the curve \( y = \sec^{2} x \) and the \(x\)-axis from \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \) to \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \).
questions.hint: Use \(\int\sec^{2}x = \tan x\); combine \(\sqrt{3}-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\).

The antiderivative of \( \sec^2 x \) is standard.
Apply the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
Substitute the limits.

questions.stem: Find the exact area enclosed between the curve \( y = \sec^{2}\!\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) \) and the \(x\)-axis from \( x = -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \) to \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \).
questions.hint: Antiderivative is \(2\tan\dfrac{x}{2}\); evaluate at \(\pm\pi/2\).

Find the antiderivative using the chain rule backwards.
Apply the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
Substitute the limits.

questions.stem: Calculate the area of the region bounded by \( y = \sin x \) and \( y = \cos x \) from \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \) to \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \).
questions.hint: Integrate upper minus lower: \(\sin x - \cos x\) from \(\pi/4\) to \(\pi/2\).

steps.explain: Identify which curve is on top in the interval \( [\pi/4, \pi/2] \). Since \( \sin x \ge \cos x \) in this region, \( y = \sin x \) is the upper curve.
Set up the definite integral for the area between the two curves.
Find the antiderivative.
Apply the limits of integration.
Substitute the upper limit \( \pi/2 \).
Substitute the lower limit \( \pi/4 \).

questions.hint: Upper curve is \(\sin x\). Antiderivative: \(-\cos x + \dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2x\).

Set up the definite integral for the enclosed area.
Find the antiderivative.
Apply the limits of integration.
Evaluate at the upper limit \( \pi/2 \) and lower limit \( \pi/3 \).

questions.hint: Integrate \(x - \sin x\); antiderivative \(\dfrac{1}{2}x^{2} + \cos x\).

steps.explain: Determine which curve is on top. Since \( x \ge \sin x \) for all \( x \ge 0 \), the line \( y = x \) is the upper boundary.
Set up the definite integral.
Find the antiderivative.
Apply the limits of integration.
Evaluate the upper and lower limits.

questions.stem: Calculate the area of the region bounded by \( y = 1 \) and \( y = \cos x \) from \( x = -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \) to \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \).
questions.hint: Integrate \(1 - \cos x\); antiderivative \(x - \sin x\).

steps.explain: Since \( \cos x \le 1 \) for all \(x\), the line \( y = 1 \) is the upper boundary.
Set up the definite integral.
Find the antiderivative.
Apply the limits of integration.
Evaluate the upper and lower limits.

questions.stem: Calculate the area of the region bounded by \( y = \sin x \), \( y = \cos x \), and the \(x\)-axis from \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \) to \( x = \pi \).
questions.hint: Split at \(\pi/2\): first between sin and cos, then under sin to the axis.

Set up the two integrals representing the two composite areas.
steps.work: A = \int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2} (\sin x - \cos x) \, dx + \int_{\pi/2}^{\pi} \sin x \, dx

steps.explain: Evaluate the first integral (area between curves).
Evaluate the second integral (area under sine).

questions.stem: The shaded region is bounded by the line \( y = x + 1 \), the curve \( y = \cos x \), and the \(x\)-axis: under the line from \( x = -1 \) to \( x = 0 \), and under the cosine from \( x = 0 \) to \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \). Find the exact area of the shaded region.
questions.hint: Split at \(x=0\): integrate \(x+1\) on \([-1,0]\) and \(\cos x\) on \([0,\pi/2]\).

steps.explain: The shaded region is composed of two distinct geometric shapes: a triangle under \( y = x + 1 \) on \( [-1, 0] \), and the area under \( y = \cos x \) on \( [0, \pi/2] \).
Calculate the area of the triangular region. This is a right triangle with base 1 and height 1.
Calculate the area of the region under the cosine curve.

questions.stem: Find the area bounded by one arch of the curve \( y = \sin x \) and the \(x\)-axis.
questions.hint: Integrate \(\sin x\) from 0 to \(\pi\).

steps.explain: One arch (half-wave) of \( y = \sin x \) begins at \( x = 0 \) and ends at \( x = \pi \).
Set up the definite integral for the area under the arch.
Find the antiderivative and apply the limits.

questions.stem: Find the area bounded by one arch of the curve \( y = \cos 2x \) and the \(x\)-axis.
questions.hint: Integrate \(\cos 2x\) over one non-negative arch, e.g. \([-\pi/4,\pi/4]\).

steps.explain: One arch (lobe) of \( y = \cos 2x \) centered on the y-axis begins at \( x = -\pi/4 \) and ends at \( x = \pi/4 \). (Alternatively, integrate from 0 to \( \pi/2 \) with absolute value).
Set up the definite integral for the area under the arch.
Find the antiderivative and apply the limits.

questions.hint: Split at \(\pi/2\) and take absolute area.

steps.explain: To find the absolute area, identify where \( y = \cos x \) crosses the \(x\)-axis. In the interval \( [0, \pi] \), it crosses at \( x = \pi/2 \).
Split the integral into two regions: positive on \( [0, \pi/2] \) and negative on \( [\pi/2, \pi] \).
Evaluate the first positive area.
Evaluate the second absolute area (negative region).

questions.stem: Find the exact value of the area enclosed between the curve \( y = \sin x \) and the \(x\)-axis from \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \) to \( x = \dfrac{3\pi}{4} \).
questions.hint: Use \(\int\sin x = -\cos x\) and exact cos of \(\pi/4\) and \(3\pi/4\).

steps.explain: On the interval \( [\pi/4, 3\pi/4] \), the curve \( y = \sin x \) is entirely above the \(x\)-axis.
Set up the definite integral directly for this interval.
Find the antiderivative and apply the limits.
Substitute the limits and evaluate. Note that \( \cos(3\pi/4) = -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \) and \( \cos(\pi/4) = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \).

questions.stem: Find the exact value of the area enclosed between the curve \( y = \cos 2x \) and the \(x\)-axis from \( x = 0 \) to \( x = \pi \).
questions.hint: Split at the zeros \(\pi/4\) and \(3\pi/4\); use absolute area.

steps.explain: Find the roots of \( y = \cos 2x \) on \( [0, \pi] \). The curve crosses the \(x\)-axis when \( 2x = \pi/2, 3\pi/2 \), so at \( x = \pi/4 \) and \( x = 3\pi/4 \).
Split the integral into three parts corresponding to the positive, negative, and positive segments.
Evaluate the first segment.
Evaluate the middle segment (absolute value).
Evaluate the final segment.

questions.stem: Find the exact value of the area enclosed between the curve \( y = \sin 2x \) and the \(x\)-axis from \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \) to \( x = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \).
questions.hint: Split at \(x=\pi/2\) where \(\sin 2x\) changes sign.

Split the integral into a positive region \( [\pi/3, \pi/2] \) and a negative region \( [\pi/2, 2\pi/3] \).
Evaluate the first part.
Evaluate the second part (absolute area).

questions.stem: Find the exact value of the area enclosed between the curve \( y = \sin x \) and the \(x\)-axis from \( x = -\dfrac{5\pi}{6} \) to \( x = \dfrac{7\pi}{6} \).
questions.hint: Interval length is \(2\pi\); absolute area of sine over a full period is 4.

steps.explain: Analyze the total length of the integration interval \( [-5\pi/6, 7\pi/6] \). The distance is \( 7\pi/6 - (-5\pi/6) = 12\pi/6 = 2\pi \).
Since \( y = \sin x \) has a period of \( 2\pi \), this interval covers exactly one full wave (two half-waves), regardless of the starting shift.
The absolute area of one half-wave (e.g., from 0 to \( \pi \)) is 2. Therefore, the absolute area over any continuous interval of \( 2\pi \) is \( 2 + 2 = 4 \).

questions.stem: Consider the curve \( y = 2\cos\pi x \) on the interval \( [-1, 1] \).

parts.stem: (a) Sketch the curve \( y = 2\cos\pi x \) on the interval \( [-1, 1] \), clearly marking the two \(x\)-intercepts.
parts.answer: Cosine wave of amplitude 2 and period 2 on \([-1,1]\): intercepts at \(x = \pm\dfrac{1}{2}\); maximum at \((0,2)\); endpoints \((\pm 1,-2)\). See solution graph.
parts.hint: Find where \(\cos\pi x = 0\) on \([-1,1]\); mark intercepts and the max/min.
parts.solution: Cosine wave of amplitude 2 and period 2 on \([-1,1]\): intercepts at \(x = \pm\dfrac{1}{2}\); maximum at \((0,2)\); endpoints \((\pm 1,-2)\). See solution graph.

steps.explain: Identify the key features of \(y = 2\cos\pi x\). Amplitude is 2 (vertical stretch by 2). Period: ordinary cos has period \(2\pi\); with argument \(\pi x\) the period is \(\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi} = 2\).

\(x\)-intercepts: set \(2\cos\pi x = 0 \Rightarrow \cos\pi x = 0 \Rightarrow \pi x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} + k\pi \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{1}{2} + k\). On the interval \([-1,1]\) the intercepts are \(x = -\dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(x = \dfrac{1}{2}\) (marked in red on the graph).
Other landmarks: at \(x = 0\), \(y = 2\) (maximum, green). At the ends of the interval, \(x = \pm 1\), \(\cos(\pm\pi) = -1\) so \(y = -2\) (minima).

Solution sketch on \([-1,1]\): a smooth cosine wave from \((-1,-2)\) up through the intercept \((-\tfrac{1}{2},0)\) to the maximum \((0,2)\), then down through \((\tfrac{1}{2},0)\) to \((1,-2)\). The two intercepts are clearly marked.

parts.stem: (b) Find the exact area bounded by the curve \( y = 2\cos\pi x \) and the \(x\)-axis, between the two \(x\)-intercepts found in part (a).
parts.hint: Integrate \(2\cos\pi x\) from \(-1/2\) to \(1/2\).
parts.solution: The correct answer is \(\dfrac{4}{\pi}\).

steps.explain: From part (a), the intercepts are \(x = -\dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(x = \dfrac{1}{2}\). On this interval \(\cos\pi x \ge 0\), so the curve is above the axis and area is simply the definite integral (no absolute value needed).
Antiderivative: \(\int 2\cos\pi x\,dx = 2\cdot\dfrac{1}{\pi}\sin\pi x = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\sin\pi x\).

steps.explain: From part (a), the intercepts are \(x = -\dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(x = \dfrac{1}{2}\). On this interval \(\cos\pi x \ge 0\), so the curve is above the axis and area is simply the definite integral (no absolute value needed).

Evaluate: \(F\!\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) - F\!\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{2}{\pi}\sin\!\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \dfrac{2}{\pi}(1) - \dfrac{2}{\pi}(-1) = \dfrac{2}{\pi} + \dfrac{2}{\pi} = \dfrac{4}{\pi}\).
Area is positive, so reject negative options. Final answer: \(\dfrac{4}{\pi}\).

questions.stem: An arch window 3 metres high and 2 metres wide is made in the shape of the curve \( y = 3\cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}x\right) \). Find the area of the window in square metres, correct to one decimal place.
questions.hint: Integrate from \(x=-1\) to \(x=1\); then approximate \(12/\pi\).

steps.explain: Width 2 m and height 3 m match the model: at \(x = 0\), \(y = 3\); the arch meets the ground where \(y = 0\), i.e. \(\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{2} = 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{\pi x}{2} = \pm\dfrac{\pi}{2} \Rightarrow x = \pm 1\). So integrate from \(-1\) to \(1\).
Antiderivative: \(\int 3\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{2}\,dx = 3\cdot\dfrac{2}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{2} = \dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{2}\).
Evaluate: \(F(1) - F(-1) = \dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\!\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \dfrac{6}{\pi}(1) - \dfrac{6}{\pi}(-1) = \dfrac{12}{\pi}\).
Numerically \(\dfrac{12}{\pi} \approx \dfrac{12}{3.1416} \approx 3.8197\), which to one decimal place is \(3.8\) m\(^2\).

questions.stem: The graphs of \( y = x - \sin x \) and \( y = x \) enclose a region. Find the total area enclosed between these graphs from \( x = 0 \) to \( x = 2\pi \).
questions.hint: The gap is \(\sin x\); use absolute value / split at \(\pi\).

steps.explain: Find the vertical distance between the two curves: \( |x - (x - \sin x)| = |\sin x| \).

Determine which curve is on top in different sub-intervals. On \( [0, \pi] \), \( \sin x \ge 0 \), so \( y = x \) is above \( y = x - \sin x \). On \( [\pi, 2\pi] \), \( \sin x \le 0 \), so \( y = x - \sin x \) is above \( y = x \).
Set up the total area as the sum of two separate integrals.
Evaluate the first integral representing the area from \( 0 \) to \( \pi \).
Evaluate the second integral representing the area from \( \pi \) to \( 2\pi \).

questions.stem: The region \(R\) is bounded by the curve \( y = \tan x \), the \(x\)-axis and the line \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \). The area of \(R\) is:
questions.hint: \(\int\tan x = -\ln|\cos x|\); evaluate from 0 to \(\pi/3\).

steps.explain: From \(x = 0\) to \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\), \(\tan x \ge 0\), so area is \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/3}\tan x\,dx\).
Write \(\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\). Substitute \(u = \cos x\), \(du = -\sin x\,dx\): \(\int\tan x\,dx = -\ln|\cos x| + C = \ln|\sec x| + C\).
Evaluate: \([-\ln\cos x]_{0}^{\pi/3} = \left(-\ln\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) - \left(-\ln\cos 0\right) = -\ln\dfrac{1}{2} + \ln 1 = -\ln\dfrac{1}{2} = \ln 2\).

questions.stem: Sketch the region bounded by the graphs of \( y = \sin x \) and \( y = \cos x \), and by the vertical lines \( x = -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \) and \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \).
questions.answer: On \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right]\), \(\cos x \ge \sin x\). Sketch both curves between the vertical lines \(x = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\); shade the region between them (see solution graph).
questions.hint: Decide which curve is above; shade between the curves and the vertical lines.
questions.solution: On \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right]\), \(\cos x \ge \sin x\). Sketch both curves between the vertical lines \(x = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\); shade the region between them (see solution graph).

steps.explain: Vertical boundaries: the region is cut off by the lines \(x = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\) (dashed in red on the diagram). Sketch both \(y = \sin x\) (indigo) and \(y = \cos x\) (green) on this interval.

Compare heights on the interval: they would meet where \(\sin x = \cos x\), i.e. at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\), which lies to the right of \(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\). So throughout \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right]\) we have \(\cos x \ge \sin x\) — cosine is the upper curve.
Mark the endpoints: at \(x = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), \(\sin = -1\) and \(\cos = 0\); at \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\), \(\sin = \dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(\cos = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).
Solution sketch: shade the band between the two curves from the left vertical line to the right (region \(R\) in the figure). This is the region whose area is found in part (b).
Final: a labelled sketch with both curves, the two vertical lines, and the shaded region between them on \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right]\).

questions.stem: Find the exact area of the region bounded by \( y = \sin x \), \( y = \cos x \), \( x = -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \) and \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \).
questions.hint: Integrate \(\cos x - \sin x\) from \(-\pi/2\) to \(\pi/6\).

steps.explain: From the sketch, area is \(\displaystyle\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/6}(\cos x - \sin x)\,dx\).
Antiderivative: \(\sin x + \cos x\) (since integral of \(-\sin x\) is \(\cos x\)).
At upper limit: \(F\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \sin\dfrac{\pi}{6} + \cos\dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).
At lower limit: \(F\!\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \sin\!\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) + \cos\!\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = -1 + 0 = -1\).

questions.stem: The curves \( y = \sin x \) and \( y = \cos 2x \) intersect at which of the following pairs of \(x\)-values (among others may exist)?
questions.hint: Use \(\cos 2x = 1 - 2\sin^{2}x\).

steps.explain: Set \(\sin x = \cos 2x\). Use the double-angle identity \(\cos 2x = 1 - 2\sin^{2}x\).
Let \(u = \sin x\): \(u = 1 - 2u^{2} \Rightarrow 2u^{2} + u - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow (2u - 1)(u + 1) = 0\). So \(u = \dfrac{1}{2}\) or \(u = -1\).
\(\sin x = -1 \Rightarrow x = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) (principal value in the usual sketching interval). \(\sin x = \dfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\) (among others).

questions.stem: On the same axes, sketch \( y = \sin x \) and \( y = \cos 2x \) on the interval \( \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\,\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right] \), marking the intersection points from part (a).
questions.answer: On \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right]\) both curves meet at the endpoints. \(\cos 2x\) is above \(\sin x\) between them. See the solution graph (shaded region \(R\)).
questions.hint: Mark the intersection points from part (a); decide which curve is above.
questions.solution: On \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right]\) both curves meet at the endpoints. \(\cos 2x\) is above \(\sin x\) between them. See the solution graph (shaded region \(R\)).

steps.explain: Interval endpoints are the intersection points from part (a): \(x = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\) (dashed red lines). Plot both curves on this closed interval.

\(y = \sin x\) (indigo): from \(\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},-1\right)\) up to \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6},\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\). \(y = \cos 2x\) (green): same left endpoint \(-1\), then rises more quickly (double angle) and meets sine again at the right endpoint.
Between the intersections, \(\cos 2x\) lies above \(\sin x\). Check at \(x = 0\): \(\cos 0 = 1 > \sin 0 = 0\). So the upper curve is cosine of double angle.
Solution sketch: both curves drawn on the interval, intersection points marked, and the region between them shaded for the area in part (c).
Final: labelled sketch with \(y = \sin x\), \(y = \cos 2x\), endpoints \(\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},-1\right)\) and \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6},\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\), and shaded region \(R\).

questions.stem: Hence find the exact area of the region bounded by \( y = \sin x \) and \( y = \cos 2x \) between their intersection points \( x = -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \) and \( x = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \).
questions.hint: Integrate \(\cos 2x - \sin x\) between the intersection points.

steps.explain: Identify which curve is on top in the interval \( [-\pi/2, \pi/6] \). At \(x=0\), \(\cos 2(0) = 1\) and \(\sin(0) = 0\). Therefore, \( y = \cos 2x \) is above \( y = \sin x \).
Set up the definite integral for the area between the curves.
Find the antiderivative of the integrand. The integral of \(\cos 2x\) is \(\frac{1}{2}\sin 2x\), and the integral of \(-\sin x\) is \(\cos x\).
Evaluate the antiderivative at the upper limit \( x = \pi/6 \).
Evaluate the antiderivative at the lower limit \( x = -\pi/2 \).

questions.stem: For every positive integer \(n\), the value of \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\pi}\sin nx\,dx\) is:
questions.hint: Find the antiderivative of \(\sin nx\), then evaluate at \(0\) and \(2\pi\).

steps.explain: To evaluate the definite integral \( \int_0^{2\pi} \sin nx \, dx \), we first find the antiderivative of \( \sin nx \).
Set up the evaluation using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
Substitute the upper limit \( x = 2\pi \). Since \(n\) is an integer, \( \cos(2n\pi) = 1 \).
Substitute the lower limit \( x = 0 \). We know \( \cos(0) = 1 \).

questions.stem: For every positive integer \(n\), the value of \(\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\pi}\cos nx\,dx\) is:
questions.hint: Antiderivative of \(\cos nx\) is \(\dfrac{1}{n}\sin nx\); evaluate at the endpoints.

steps.explain: To evaluate the definite integral \( \int_0^{2\pi} \cos nx \, dx \), we first find the antiderivative of \( \cos nx \).
Set up the evaluation using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
Substitute the upper limit \( x = 2\pi \). Since \(n\) is an integer, \( \sin(2n\pi) = 0 \).
Substitute the lower limit \( x = 0 \). We know \( \sin(0) = 0 \).

questions.stem: Find the area between the curve \( y = \sin x \) and the \(x\)-axis from \( x = 0 \) to \( x = 2\pi \).
questions.hint: Use absolute area: split at \(x=\pi\) where \(\sin x\) changes sign.

steps.explain: The function \( y = \sin x \) crosses the \(x\)-axis at \( x = \pi \) on the interval \( [0, 2\pi] \).
On \( [0, \pi] \), \( \sin x \ge 0 \). On \( [\pi, 2\pi] \), \( \sin x \le 0 \). We must split the integral to find the absolute area.
Evaluate the first half-wave (positive area).
Evaluate the second half-wave (absolute value of negative area).

questions.stem: Find the area between the curve \( y = \sin 2x \) and the \(x\)-axis from \( x = 0 \) to \( x = 2\pi \).
questions.hint: Absolute area of \(|\sin 2x|\) on \([0,2\pi]\); four half-waves each of area 1.

steps.explain: The function \( y = \sin 2x \) has a period of \( \frac{2\pi}{2} = \pi \). In the interval \( [0, 2\pi] \), there are exactly \(2\) full periods, yielding \(4\) half-waves.
We find the area of a single half-wave by integrating over one positive section, from \(0\) to \( \frac{\pi}{2} \).
Evaluate this integral.

questions.stem: Find the area between the curve \( y = \sin 3x \) and the \(x\)-axis from \( x = 0 \) to \( x = 2\pi \).
questions.hint: Absolute area of \(|\sin 3x|\); six half-waves each of area \(\dfrac{2}{3}\).

steps.explain: The function \( y = \sin 3x \) has a period of \( \frac{2\pi}{3} \). Over the interval \( [0, 2\pi] \), there are exactly \(3\) full periods, resulting in \(6\) half-waves.
We find the area of a single half-wave by integrating from \(0\) to \( \frac{\pi}{3} \).
Evaluate this integral.

questions.stem: Find the area between the curve \( y = \sin nx \) and the \(x\)-axis from \( x = 0 \) to \( x = 2\pi \) (\(n\) a positive integer).
questions.hint: For integer \(n\): \(2n\) half-waves each of area \(\dfrac{2}{n}\) gives total area 4.

steps.explain: The function \( y = \sin nx \) has a period of \( \frac{2\pi}{n} \). Over the interval \( [0, 2\pi] \), there are exactly \(n\) full periods, which means there are \(2n\) identical half-waves.
The area of a single half-wave is the integral from \(0\) to \( \frac{\pi}{n} \).
Evaluate this integral for a general integer \(n\).

steps.explain: Split the definite integral into two separate parts using the linearity of integration.
Evaluate the first integral (which geometrically represents the area of a rectangle of height 1 and width \(n\)).
Analyze the second integral. The function \( \sin 2\pi x \) has a period of \( \frac{2\pi}{2\pi} = 1 \). Integrating from 0 to integer \(n\) means integrating over exactly \(n\) full periods.
The integral of a sine wave over any full period is zero, because the positive and negative regions completely cancel out.

questions.stem: Sketch \( y = 1 + \sin 2\pi x \) for \( 0 \le x \le n \) (positive integer \(n\)), and interpret the result of part (a) geometrically.
questions.answer: Sketch of \(y = 1 + \sin 2\pi x\): period 1, range \([0,2]\), about the line \(y=1\). Each unit interval has area 1 under the curve, so total area from 0 to \(n\) is \(n\), matching part (a).
questions.hint: Period is 1; sketch a few periods and link each unit area to part (a).
questions.solution: The graph is a sine wave of period 1 shifted up by 1 (range \([0,2]\)). It never goes below the \(x\)-axis. Over each interval \([k,k+1]\) the area under the curve is 1. Hence from 0 to \(n\) the total area is \(n\), which is exactly the value of the integral in part (a).

steps.explain: Analyze the function \( y = 1 + \sin 2\pi x \). It is a sine wave with amplitude 1, shifted up by 1 unit. Its period is \( \frac{2\pi}{2\pi} = 1 \), and its range is \( [0, 2] \).

Sketching the graph: it starts at \( (0, 1) \), reaches a maximum of 2 at \( x = 0.25 \), crosses 1 at \( x = 0.5 \), reaches a minimum of 0 at \( x = 0.75 \), and completes one cycle at \( (1, 1) \). This repeats \(n\) times.
Since the curve never drops below the \(x\)-axis (minimum is 0), the definite integral exactly represents the absolute area under the curve.

parts.stem: (a) Find the intersection points of \( y=\sin x \) and \( y=\cos x \) in the domain \( 0\le x\le 2\pi \).

steps.explain: At an intersection point, the two functions have the same y-value, so set \( \sin x=\cos x \).
Divide both sides by \( \cos x \) to obtain a single trigonometric function. (This is valid since \( \sin x \) and \( \cos x \) are never zero at the same time).
Using the ASTC (All Stations To Central) rule, determine which quadrants \( \tan x \) is positive in. Since \( \tan x = +1 \), our solutions must lie in the 1st (All) and 3rd (Tan) quadrants.
Find the base angle in the 1st quadrant, and then use it to find the corresponding angle in the 3rd quadrant (by adding \( \pi \)).
We can confirm these two intersection points visually by graphing \( y = \sin x \) (blue) and \( y = \cos x \) (red). The curves intersect exactly twice between \( 0 \) and \( 2\pi \).

parts.stem: (b) Using the intersection points from part (a), find the exact area bounded by \( y=\sin x \) and \( y=\cos x \) from \( x=\dfrac{\pi}{4} \) to \( x=\dfrac{5\pi}{4} \).

steps.explain: Between \( x=\dfrac{\pi}{4} \) and \( x=\dfrac{5\pi}{4} \), \( \sin x \ge \cos x \) (check at \( x=\pi/2 \): \( \sin=1>\cos=0 \)). So the area is the integral of the upper curve minus the lower curve.
Find the primitive of \( \sin x-\cos x \).
Evaluate the primitive at the upper limit \( x=\dfrac{5\pi}{4} \), using \( \cos\dfrac{5\pi}{4}=\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{4}=-\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2} \).
Evaluate the primitive at the lower limit \( x=\dfrac{\pi}{4} \), using \( \cos\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2} \), then subtract.
Part (a): find intersection points of \(y=\sin x\) and \(y=\cos x\) by setting them equal and solving for \(x\) in \([0,2\pi]\).
Solve \(\tan x = 1\) within \([0, 2\pi]\), where tangent is positive in quadrants 1 and 3.
steps.work: \(x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\) (quadrant 1), \(x = \pi + \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{5\pi}{4}\) (quadrant 3)\\ Both lie in \([0,2\pi]\), confirming the intersections at \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) and \(x=\dfrac{5\pi}{4}\).

questions.stem: Convert \(5^\circ\) to radians in exact form.
questions.hint: Use the small-angle approximations \(\sin x \approx x\) and \(\tan x \approx x\) when \(x\) is in radians and small.

steps.explain: Use \(180^\circ = \pi\) radians: \(5^\circ = 5 \times \dfrac{\pi}{180} = \dfrac{5\pi}{180}\).
Simplify by dividing numerator and denominator by 5: \(\dfrac{\pi}{36}\).
Final answer: \(\dfrac{\pi}{36}\).

questions.stem: Which statement is correct for the small-angle approximations used in this section?
options: If \(x\) is small and measured in radians, then \(\sin x \approx x\) and \(\tan x \approx x\).
If \(x\) is small and measured in degrees, then \(\sin x \approx x\).
​\(\sin x \approx x\) is valid for all real \(x\).
Only \(\cos x \approx x\) is used for small angles.
questions.hint: Use the small-angle approximations \(\sin x \approx x\) and \(\tan x \approx x\) when \(x\) is in radians and small.
questions.solution: If \(x\) is small and measured in radians, then \(\sin x \approx x\) and \(\tan x \approx x\).

steps.explain: On the unit circle, a small central angle \(x\) (radians) has arc length \(x\). The vertical chord and the tangent segment are both nearly equal to that arc when \(x\) is small.
Hence the standard approximations: \(\sin x \approx x\) and \(\tan x \approx x\) for small \(x\) in radians. (Also \(\cos x \approx 1\), not \(x\).)
These fail if \(x\) is left in degrees. Final answer: the statement that requires radians.

parts.solution: The correct answer is \(\dfrac{\pi}{60}\).

steps.explain: Given: convert \(3^\circ\) to radians. Strategy: use the exact conversion \(180^\circ = \pi\) radians, so multiply by \(\dfrac{\pi}{180}\).
Multiply: \(3^\circ = 3 \times \dfrac{\pi}{180} = \dfrac{3\pi}{180}\).

Simplify the fraction: divide numerator and denominator by 3 to get \(\dfrac{\pi}{60}\). A common slip is writing \(\dfrac{\pi}{30}\) (as if converting \(6^\circ\)) or inverting the conversion factor.
Final answer: \(\dfrac{\pi}{60}\).

parts.stem: Which statement correctly explains why \(\sin 3^\circ \approx \dfrac{\pi}{60}\)?
options: For small \(x\) in radians, \(\sin x \approx x\). Since \(3^\circ = \dfrac{\pi}{60}\) rad, \(\sin 3^\circ \approx \dfrac{\pi}{60}\).
For small \(x\) in degrees, \(\sin x \approx x\), so \(\sin 3^\circ \approx 3\).
Always \(\sin \theta = \theta\) in any unit, so the value equals the degree measure.
Use \(\sin x \approx \dfrac{\pi}{180}\) for every angle near the origin.
parts.hint: Use the small-angle approximations \(\sin x \approx x\) and \(\tan x \approx x\) when \(x\) is in radians and small.
parts.solution: For small \(x\) in radians, \(\sin x \approx x\). Since \(3^\circ = \dfrac{\pi}{60}\) rad, \(\sin 3^\circ \approx \dfrac{\pi}{60}\).

steps.explain: Key fact (small-angle approximation): when \(x\) is measured in radians and is close to 0, \(\sin x \approx x\). (This fails if \(x\) is left in degrees.)
From the previous part, \(3^\circ = \dfrac{\pi}{60}\) radians. The angle is small (about 0.052 rad), so the approximation is appropriate.
Therefore \(\sin 3^\circ = \sin\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{60}\right) \approx \dfrac{\pi}{60}\). A common mistake is applying \(\sin x \approx x\) with \(x\) still in degrees (which would wrongly give 3).
Final answer: the statement that uses radians and \(\sin x \approx x\).

parts.stem: Taking \(\pi = 3.142\), find \(\sin 3^\circ\) correct to four decimal places, without using the sine key on a calculator.
parts.hint: Use the small-angle approximations \(\sin x \approx x\) and \(\tan x \approx x\) when \(x\) is in radians and small.
parts.solution: The correct answer is \(0.0524\).

steps.explain: From the small-angle result: \(\sin 3^\circ \approx \dfrac{\pi}{60}\). Use the given value \(\pi = 3.142\).
Round to four decimal places: the fifth decimal digit is 6, so round up from 0.0523 to \(0.0524\). A common slip is stopping at 0.0523 or shifting the decimal point to 0.524.
Final answer: \(0.0524\).

questions.hint: Work through the parts in order. Convert degrees to radians before using \(\sin x \approx x\).

questions.stem: Using \(\sin x \approx x\) with \(x\) in radians, approximate \(\sin 2^\circ\) to four decimal places. Take \(\pi = 3.142\).
questions.hint: Use the small-angle approximations \(\sin x \approx x\) and \(\tan x \approx x\) when \(x\) is in radians and small.

steps.explain: Convert: \(2^\circ = 2 \times \dfrac{\pi}{180} = \dfrac{\pi}{90}\).
Approximate: \(\sin 2^\circ \approx \dfrac{\pi}{90} = \dfrac{3.142}{90} = 0.034911\ldots\).
To four decimal places: \(0.0349\).

questions.stem: A kite string is \(80\,\text{m}\) long and makes an angle of \(3^\circ\) with the horizontal. Approximately how high is the kite above the ground? Use \(\sin x \approx x\) (radians) and give the answer to the nearest metre.
questions.hint: Use the small-angle approximations \(\sin x \approx x\) and \(\tan x \approx x\) when \(x\) is in radians and small.

steps.explain: Height \(h = 80\sin 3^\circ\). Convert: \(3^\circ = \dfrac{\pi}{60}\) rad, so \(\sin 3^\circ \approx \dfrac{\pi}{60}\).
Simplify: \(h \approx \dfrac{80\pi}{60} = \dfrac{4\pi}{3} \approx \dfrac{4 \times 3.1416}{3} \approx 4.19\,\text{m}\).
Nearest metre: \(4\,\text{m}\).

questions.stem: A car travels \(2\,\text{km}\) up a road inclined at \(4^\circ\) to the horizontal. Through what vertical distance has the car climbed? Use \(\sin x \approx x\) for small angles in radians, and give your answer correct to the nearest metre.
questions.hint: Use the small-angle approximations \(\sin x \approx x\) and \(\tan x \approx x\) when \(x\) is in radians and small.

steps.explain: Given: road length (hypotenuse) \(2\,\text{km} = 2000\,\text{m}\), inclination \(4^\circ\). Unknown: vertical climb \(h\). Sketch a right triangle with hypotenuse along the road.
In the right triangle, \(\sin 4^\circ = \dfrac{h}{2000}\), so \(h = 2000\sin 4^\circ\).
Convert the angle to radians: \(4^\circ = 4 \times \dfrac{\pi}{180} = \dfrac{\pi}{45}\). For small angles, \(\sin x \approx x\) (radians), so \(\sin 4^\circ \approx \dfrac{\pi}{45}\).
Hence \(h \approx 2000 \times \dfrac{\pi}{45} = \dfrac{2000\pi}{45} = \dfrac{400\pi}{9}\). Using \(\pi \approx 3.1416\): \(\dfrac{400 \times 3.1416}{9} \approx 139.63\,\text{m}\).
Nearest metre: \(140\,\text{m}\). A common slip is leaving the answer in kilometres, or using \(\tan\) instead of \(\sin\) with the road length as the adjacent side.
Final answer: \(140\,\text{m}\).

questions.stem: A tower is \(40\,\text{m}\) high. What angle, correct to the nearest minute, does it subtend at a point \(5\,\text{km}\) away on level ground? Use \(\tan x \approx x\) for small \(x\) in radians.
questions.hint: Use the small-angle approximations \(\sin x \approx x\) and \(\tan x \approx x\) when \(x\) is in radians and small.

steps.explain: Given: tower height \(40\,\text{m}\), horizontal distance \(5\,\text{km} = 5000\,\text{m}\). Let \(\theta\) be the angle subtended at the observer (angle of elevation of the top of the tower).
From the right triangle: \(\tan \theta = \dfrac{40}{5000} = \dfrac{1}{125} = 0.008\).
The angle is small, so in radians \(\tan \theta \approx \theta\). Therefore \(\theta \approx 0.008\) radians.
Convert to degrees: \(\theta \approx 0.008 \times \dfrac{180}{\pi} \approx 0.008 \times 57.296 \approx 0.4584^\circ\).

Convert the decimal part of a degree to minutes: \(0.4584 \times 60 \approx 27.5'\), which rounds to \(28'\) to the nearest minute. A common slip is converting to degrees only, or using \(\sin\) with the wrong side ratio.
Final answer: \(28'\).

questions.stem: The moon subtends an angle of \(32'\) at an observation point on Earth, \(380\,000\,\text{km}\) away. Treating the moon's diameter as approximately an arc of a circle centred at the observer, find the approximate diameter of the moon to the nearest kilometre.
questions.hint: Use the small-angle approximations \(\sin x \approx x\) and \(\tan x \approx x\) when \(x\) is in radians and small.

steps.explain: Given: subtended angle \(\theta = 32'\), distance (radius) \(r = 380\,000\,\text{km}\). Approximate diameter \(D\) by arc length \(s = r\theta\) with \(\theta\) in radians.
Convert minutes to degrees: \(32' = \dfrac{32}{60}^\circ = \dfrac{8}{15}^\circ\).
Convert to radians: \(\theta = \dfrac{8}{15} \times \dfrac{\pi}{180} = \dfrac{8\pi}{2700} = \dfrac{2\pi}{675}\).
Arc length (approximate diameter): \(D \approx r\theta = 380\,000 \times \dfrac{2\pi}{675}\).
Simplify: \(\dfrac{760\,000}{675} = \dfrac{30400}{27}\approx 1125.926\), then multiply by \(\pi\approx 3.1416\) to get \(D \approx 3537.4\,\text{km}\). To the nearest kilometre: \(3537\,\text{km}\).
Final answer: \(3537\,\text{km}\). A common slip is leaving \(\theta\) in degrees when using \(s = r\theta\).

questions.stem: A regular polygon with \(360\) sides is inscribed in a circle of radius \(80\,\text{cm}\). Find the approximate length of each side, correct to two decimal places. (Use the small-angle arc approximation.)
questions.hint: Use the small-angle approximations \(\sin x \approx x\) and \(\tan x \approx x\) when \(x\) is in radians and small.

steps.explain: Given: regular 360-gon inscribed in a circle of radius \(r = 80\,\text{cm}\). Each central angle is \(\dfrac{360^\circ}{360} = 1^\circ\). Approximate each side by the corresponding arc length.
In radians: \(1^\circ = \dfrac{\pi}{180}\). Arc length \(s = r\theta = 80 \times \dfrac{\pi}{180} = \dfrac{80\pi}{180} = \dfrac{4\pi}{9}\).
Numerically: \(\dfrac{4\pi}{9} \approx \dfrac{4 \times 3.1416}{9} \approx \dfrac{12.5664}{9} \approx 1.3963\,\text{cm}\).
Correct to two decimal places: \(1.40\,\text{cm}\). A common slip is using the chord formula with a half-angle without approximating, or forgetting to convert to radians.
Final answer: \(1.40\,\text{cm}\).
